THE RAINBOW. • "Where are you going, my little maid?" " After the rainbow, sir," she said; • "Alter the rainbow, yellow, blue, red, ;„ After the rainbow, sir," she said. F " Where shall you &id it, my little maid f" ▪ " Over the hill there, sir," she said ; L "It touches the ground with its blue and red, ; Over the hill there, sir," she said. • "What do you want with it, my little maid?" "The crock that it points to, sir," she said. r "A crock of gold pieces, yellow and red; • The crock that it points to, sir," she said, r *What will you do with it, my little maid ?" Buy a great wax doll, sir," she said "With eyes so blue, and with cheeks so red; k▪ /II buy a great wax doll, sir," she said, • "You'll never find it, my little maid." yes, I shall, good sir," she said; "Just where the ground is yellow and red, I. Where the rainbow touches the ground," she said. r Over the hill went the little maid, After the rainbow, yellow and red; I But she never found it, lam afraid; No, she never found it, so people said. ▪ Btu Peep" for March. •

FOR EVER AND AYE. In the soften'd light of a summer eve, In the shelter'd nook of a woodland dell, Where the late bee linger'd, loth to leave, The last faint rays of the sunlight fell Over her face, so fair, so sweet— . Over his words so free and fond: Ah, never before we the hours so fleet, Never a vision so bright beyond— " Love, come what must, or come what may, I will be true for ever and aye !" Into a far land wander'd he, • A soldier seeking to win renown; And whether he sought it—shore or sea— By lonely desert or leaguer'd town, , There follow'd ev.er a woman's prayer; - And be he distant, or be he dead, She hearken'd his words in the silent air And softly the echoes whispered— • "Love, come what must, or come what may, I will be true for ever and aye l" In the dim light of cathedral aisles • A valiant warrior weds his bride, • A rich, proud lady, full of smiles— • Proud of the hero by her side. Who, knAelini at the altar rail, Where fall the organ's deep'ning tones, Hears not you crouching, crush'd one's wail— Reeds not The words she, sobbing, moans— "Oh, come What must, or come what may, Were you not mine for ever and aye?" Into the depths ot the silent night, •

Hp to the great white throne on high, A weary, spirit hath winged its flight— A broken heart at his door doth lie; For so women trust, and so men vow, And the world wags on in careless glee. Till the stricken of heart, forsaken now, Seeks a haven of rest where, perchance, there be— Let come what must, or come what may— Hearts leal and true for ever and aye! 4--London Society.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 21 1885' WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present— Messrs. Greening (chairman), Caldwell, Appleton, Brown, Cooper, William Houghton, Ratcliffe, Jolley, Mackie, Boa- nel I, Jeans, Grange, Greenall, Gibsan, Derbyshire, Rev G. F. Roberts, OweneForater; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk). TRH CATHOLIC CHILDR.EN AT PADOATE On the minutee of the Schools Committee coming up for confirmation, Mr. CALDWELL mentioued that the Catholic) children at Padgett, schools had not attended their cbapel for many Sundays, because the officials who woteld have to take charge of chain objected to go to a Catholic chapel. He did not blame them for this, leecause they objected ea principle, bet he suggested that some arrangement be made which would enable the children to attend the chapel.—Mr Bletcx.nuseer said he quite sympathised with what Mr. Cald- well said. It was the case, he believed, at every other in- dustrial school that children attended the chapels of their own denominations, and he thought some mach arrangement as that proposed by Mr. Caldwell should be made. It was one of those cases, he thought, that might be lift to the ' committee to deal with at their next meeting.—Mr. Caere WELL had no objection to the matter being referred to the committee, and that was accordingly done. AN INSURED pIUPER. In the minutes of the House Committee It was stated that the Master of the Workhouse reported the death of James Jones, whose life he was informed had been insured to a large amount, say £loo—Mr. SIIHARER erelieving officer) said that he had made some inquiries, and he was informed that the deceased had been insured by another man in the Prudential Assurance Society. If he were instructed by the Board he would make a claim for about a year's maintesance.—Mr. Shearer was instructed to take the requi- site steps for making the claim. SCHOOL FEES. The School Fees Committee reported that they had dealt with 76 old and 27 new cases.—Mr Beemeanner moved the adoption ot these minutes.—Dr MACKIE, in seconding, said he would take that opportunity of congratulating the chair- man on the honour her Majesty's Government had been pleased to confer upon him in appointing him a magistrate. They looked upon that appointment with more than ordin- ary delight as he was their chairman. (Hear, bear.) Re- ferring to the school fees, Dr Mackie said that a discussion had taken place in the Warrington Town Council on school fees, and several Town Councillors seemed to think that they as a School Fees Committee might do a little more than they did ; he thought they even suggested that some- thing in the shape of shoes, eec, might be given. He no- ticed that the fees of Warrington and Latchford amounted to £1.19 a year, whilst in Newton they ran their fees up to £129. Newton was a much smaller township, and it might be presumed that out of that large amount they gave some- thing besides school fees. At all events he should like t 9 have some information as to how they managed to expend that five-fold amount he might call it in proportion to pope.; Litton, as it might be a good example to show them how they might indulge a little more the poor people who asked their assistance. He also referred to the high rates of War- rington, and advocated a mode of assessment which would tend to relieve the shopkeepers and farmers by making people pay more according to their means.—Mr AETLETON said that at Newton they never granted applicants anything more than school fees. He believed the greater portion of their school fees were paid to Haydock people. The weevil at Havdock were very low now' and there were a great many men on short time, and the consequence was that there were many school fees to pay.--Mr JOLLEE said that in giving these fees they had to use the machinery they had. He quite agreed with Dr Mackie that a better system ought to be adopted, but at present they had no power to give shoes or clogs or anything except school fees.—Mr CALDWELL said that at Newton they appeared to be a very quarrelsome lot. eleaughter.) What with anti-vaccinators, bye-elec- tions, expensive medicines, high school fees, and vaccine- time fees that Board had more trouble with them than with all the rest of the Union put together. An explanation that had been given by Mr Shearer why the school fees at New- ton were so heavy, was that after they had inquired into a case they put it down for about 20 weeks. In Warrington they were more careful, and only put the cases down for three or four weeks, and sometimes less. He believed that ultimately the cost of education would be met by a national tax. (Hear, hear.) If instead of spending meney on petty wars, fighting nig- gers and such like—(laughter)—the Government would hand over two or three millions for edneation it would, be a good thing. (Hear, hear.) It would be a good thing to have education free, and to let every parent bring up his children in his own way of thinking. (Hear, hear.)—Mr RATCLIFFE was sorry that Newton was the black spot in the Warrington Union. He considered that the names of those parties who received school fees ought to be read over. (" No, no.") He thought so, although he would be one of the last persons to prevent poor people from getting school fees if they deeeryed them.—The CLERK said it had been considered a very dangerous thing to accompany school fees With any other kind of relief. If they did, they would be inundated with applications from persons very well able to pay for themselves. With regard to assessments the Clerk also mentioned that up to the time of Lord Mans- field the poor rates were made according to the ability to pay.- Mr. JEANS thought the time had come when landowners and cconpiers should make some effort to improve the mode of rating at present in use. All kinds of expenses were thrown upon the poor-rate, which was upon land, and he thought it was quite time that farmers and landowners should set in mot:oa an agitation with a view of getting that sort of thing altered. He did not see why persons having a large amount of personal property should not Contribute to the poor rate.—Mr BLACKIIIIRST pointed out that the committee could not grant anything to applicants which sympathy might dictate, as they were bound down by law as to what they had to give.—The minutes were then confirmed. SIUNDAY CLOSING. The consideration of a petition for Sunday Closing was left over till the next meeting to allow of all members who desired to take part in the discussion a chance of being present. VACCINATION AT BIIRTONWOOD. A letter was read from Dr. Watkins stating that there would be speciel attendances next Tuesday, at Burtonwood, for vaccination and re-vaccination. THE BOARD AND THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS. The CLERK said with regard to the expected litigation between the Guardians and Newton Commissioners, he had two letters from Meesrs Jeans and Co., the solicitors of the Guardians. The first letter dated 14th March was as fol- lows —"We: had a call from Mr Worsley yesterday. He threw out the hint or offer that the amount in question should be divided and the Guardians pay one-half. As the claim involves a principle and as we deny the liability in tato we cannot advise any such compromise, but we inform you of the offer in case you think it well to mention it to the Board." The other letter. dated March 16th, was as follows:—" Mr 'Woreley says that in two or three cases the Guardians bwe acted on the principles laid down in your letter of March 1881, and he says he relies on those cases as evidence of the Guardians having recognised and acted on your letter as an agreement. We do not agree with that conclusion as a matter of law. We should like, however, to have informed what cases you have had with the Newton Commissioners since March 1881, and the facts of such cases so that we may know what bearing they may have on the case of Harris."—Mr JEANS said that he had put the whole facts before the barrister he bad engaged to conduct the case, and he had ' advised in the same way that he (Mr Jeans) Ind previously advised the Board. He then read the barrister's opinion as follows "I have not the slightest hesitation in arriving at the opinion that plaintiffs cannot recover in this case. The case is moreover exceedingly simple. Plaintiffs have cer- tain statutory powers and responsibilities, and among the latter a responsibility to pay for persons who are by a cer- tain process taken to hospitals provided for that purpose. Section 124 of the Publie Health Act, 1875, only deals with the cost of removing, and this cost must be altogether borne by the local authority, but Inca:in 132 provides for the cost of maintenance also, and enables the local authority to re- cover from the patient if not a pauper. The consent of the superintendent body of the hospital is required, and this is no doubt intended to meet cases where there is no general contract between the Local Authority and the Hospital. The whole question is one of contract. There is no duty on the part of the Guardians in law, nor as far as I can see is there any suggestion by plaintiffs of a duty on the part of the Guardians. That there is no special contract is equally clear on the evidence. The patients were not paupers, and the Guardians have no power to enter into such a contract. It is beyond their province. But even suppose it was the duty of the Guardians to do what the Commissioners have done, it is not competent for the Commissioners to do the Guardians' work and charge them for it. The Guardians have duties to perform within their discretion, and the Commissioners are not the persona to exercise that discre- tion for thean."—Mr. BIACKIIIIRST asked when the case would come before tbe court—Mr. JEANS nip next Thurs- day, unless the plaintiffs showed the better part of valour. —Mr. Deeteesniee said he was glad to hear the barrister's opinion read, and he was also glad that Mr. Jeans had net consented to a compromise.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said that was another black spot against Newton. (Laughter.) It seemed to him that case would touch the ratepayers of Newton whichever wey it went. . He did hope that the Commis- sioners would think better of it, and not go on with the litigation.—Mr.- JEANS should think they would think better of it, because they had not a leg to stand on. He had noticed in the report of toe Newton Commissioners meeting that a member of the Board of Commissioners, who was an cr officio Guardiara, too, said that he did not see why the Guardians objected to pay, the amount. He (Mr. Jeans) should think the Guardians would be very silly people in- deed if they paid every claim nude against them without any legal foundation whatever. It was was not for them to pay all sorts of claims made against them unless legally bound.—The subject then dropped. A RELIEF OFFICE. A letter was read from Mr. T. J. ; brushes,coffins, THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. dothingpt POULTRY AT THE ROYAL SHOW. ' Some time ago'we announced that the Royal Agricul- tural Society had, largely in answer to the petition first I proposed in this column, decided to add poultry classes I to t4eir text Show, which is to be held in the Moor Park 7uly. This step is not a little remarkable, as the ,Cduncil-have for years refused to take this step, is,ff repeatedly urged to do so by those interested VI-thd poultry question. Some years ago it was thought • that it would be done at the Reading Show, but the effort did no succeed. The reasons for this refusal to add what even the Royal Council acknowledge to be an important part of farm stock, and one which deserves encouragement at their hands, as evinced by the articles given from time to time in the Society's journal, may be stated as three-fold—First, they thought the time of year at which the Show is held—July--to be unsuitable for a poultry show, and there can be no question but that it is not the most suitable time. Still a good show can then be got together, we are sure. Second, some seventeen or eighteen years ago poultry were added to the Bury St. Edmunds Show, and as that was a dismal failure the Council were reluctant to try again, forget- ting that the failure was largely due to their own bad arrangements, and that some of the conditions made thereat were a direct hindrance to exhibitors. And third, which perhaps was the strongest reason of all, the Royal Agricultural Society hold the opinion that the pre- sent system of poultry shows is a mistake, not conducive to the interests of poultry keeping generally as a good- producing pursuit; and they were unwilling to add another fanciers' show to the large number already in existence. Until they could see some plan which would prevent their show being merely a fanciers' exhibition they refused to entertain the idea at all. We think they have got hold of an erroneous idea, but this is not the place to contest it. Like most ideas, there is some truth in their contention, but in dwelling upon the minor truth they are blind to other and overwhelming facts. However, some months ago, when the agitation was started for the purpose of inducing the Council to add poultry to the Preston Show, so strong was the pressure that they yielded, with the result that we have now be- fore us a list of prizes offered for the meeting which opens on the 15th of July next. This schedule is marked by several features which at once give it an iddividuality not possessed by any other British show. It is. in fact, much on the lines of the show held at Paris a month ago. Whether it will be as great a success as it would otherwise have been, had it followed the regular path, may be questioned. To make great fundamental changes seldom succeeds at first, and we shall be very curious indeed to learn the result of this experiment If it is successful, the probabilities are that the example will be followed by most of the agri- cultural societies. If it is unsuccessful, a very heavy blow will be dealt at those who seek to develop the poul- try interest from an economical point of view. Although we are very strongly of opinion that the Royal Council would have acted more wisely had they at first followed the old lines of shows, we hope this experiment will not fail. The question is of too much importance to permit predilections to rule. And though its failure should re- sult, the Council will have no one to blame but them- selves, that would be nit: poor consolation to those who have the question at heart. We hope, therefore, every- one in this district will supportthe show to the best of their ability. We are very glad to see the liberality in respect to prizes, of which there are three in each of the classes given, namely :—First prize, £3; second prize, £2; and third prize, £l. This means £3OO in prizes for this section alone. The entry fees are small. Those who are members of the society have to pay only half-a- crown for each entry, but non-members will be charged five shillings. The sum is a very small one, considering the prizes. At such shows as the Crystal Palace, Bir- mingham, and the Dairy, in many classes the prizes are £2, £l, and 10s., the entry fee eight shillings, so that relatively, if this were the only question, there should be a much larger entry at Preston. Such prizes should. tempt exhibitors, and make them respond heartily. The classes number 50 in all, 25 of which are for odd birds, i.e., those hatched previous to January Ist, 1885, and 25 for chickens, i.e., hatched after January Ist, 1885. Whilst acknowledging that it is wise ,to encourage the early hatching of chickens, we believe these young bird classes to be a mistake. Most of the:chickens shown will be hatched during March and April (as the schedule has only been issued in March there has been no incen- tive to earlier hatching), and if we take March 15th as a mean, the chickens shown will only be 17 weeks old. To keep birds of this age, especially as both sexes are in one pen, in a confined space seven days, can only be characterised as gross cruelty, and we are very much surprised that the Council of the Royal have boen so ill- advised as to adopt such a plan as this. We shall not be surprised if the chicken classes prove a failure. The classes are divided as follows :—Brahmas, 4 classes; Cochins, 2 ; Langshans, 2 ; Houdans, 2;• Plymouth Rocks, 2; Andalusians, 2; Hamburghs, 4; Leghorns, 2; Polish, 2; Black ,Spanish, 2; Dorkings, 6 ; Creves, 2; Game (in which the sexes are divided), 8; ducks, 4; geese, 2; and turkeys, 4. We can 'only find two faults with this arrangement, both 'of which are seldom,. how- ever. The first is, Black Minorcas are entirely omitted. This is the most valuable of our laying breeds, and to omit itis a very serious matter, especially as there is no any. Ober Variety class. It is now popular in this dis- trict, and the reports Oféil 11,7 readers of Tiff quardfon have shown its value. The second is that classes, both. pure arid -crossed, for table poultry, to .be killed during the -show, have not been given. These would have proved not only most interesting, but the most instruc- tive feature of the show. We regret exceedingly that they have not been given especially as we know the Council were urged to include both Minoreas and table poultry. The great changeniado is that every Pen :(except the Game) must contain a cock and three hens.. This was the custom a generation ago. Then the number was re- duced to a eduple of hens, and finally to One of each sex. The return to what has become an obsolete custom is a doubtful policy, and, relied upon as it is to discourage fanciers, and eucotgage farmers, will not, we think, work to that end. Faikiers, more than farmers, can make tip a goocYquartette of their special breed or breeds. No one can exhibit more than two pens in any one class. There are alterations in the rules which are decided improvements, and as the society will rigidly carry these out, exhibitors should !carefully study the conditions. Every exhibit must be the property of the exhibitor at the time of entry, and on the first day of exhibition; ,the 'age must be stated; disqualifications will tot only affect the bird so dealt with, but '!,the whole of the exhibits belonging to the same exhibitor, will be labelled disqualified, whether exhibited in the same class or in other classes ;" fines will, be imposed upon exhibitors for (1) the exhibition of birds suffering from contagious or infectious diseases, {2) fer incorrectness of certificates, and (3) for the entry but-non-exhibition (except for specified reasons) .of birds. It is also provided that no person who -Shalt have been to the satisfaction of the Council to have beervezcluded from exhibiting for prizes, at Pima exhibition of any other society in con.se- quence &Mixing attempted to•obtain a prize by giving a false certificate, shall be allowed to exhibit at this or any other show of the society. The instructions to the judges state that high condition, quality, purity of race, and weight will be taken into consideration by the judges in a greater degree than mere beauty of plumage _without these distinctions; and also that the judges of -poultry will take into consideration the ages of poultry sent for competition, aitd if perfectly satisfied that in any case, the age has been incorrectly stated, they are empowered, with the sanction of the stewards, to dis- qualify such entries; and no appeals from the decision of the judges will be, entertained upon any grounds whatever.

COTTAGE iGARDENING Ceoeriwa Gitorria6.—However mad the garden ma be, there should be a systematic coarse of cropping: The same crop should by no means occupy the same piece of ground successively. We do not assert that it will not grow, as we have proved to tho contrary; but we do maintain that a crop of a different nature will succeed better. We have grown Celery on a piece of ground for four successive seasons and the last was the best. Here we took no intermediate crop, and the Celery received a fresh supply of manure each season, and was also planted a good distance apart, so that it did not depend on Its supply of food from the same source annually. Each year the position of the ridges was also changed. The cultivator should, however, avoid introducing the same crop or even those related to it on the same piece of ground two years in succes- sion, unless he is well supplied with manure. Cabbage, Cauliflowers, Broccoli, and all kinds of kales are one family, and equally exhaustive. Peas and Beans of all kinds form another class. Parsley, Parsnip, Carrots, and Celery belong to the umbelliferous family, a designa- tion which indicates the form of the flower heads. Most things may, however, be planted after Celery, as the roots only traverse but a portion of the soil. Con- sequently, as a matter of convenience, many good gar- ' donors devote the Celery ground to Onions, Carrots, and Parsnip. Celery ridges should be levelled and the ground trod transverse, when it will be lower at the spaces between and require further levelling and after- wards forked over, at the same time keeping a sharp look out that no irregularities are formed. Some gar- deners occupy the Celery ground with Peas, and before levelling takes place a stick should be inserted in the aentre of the ridge so that the Peas may be sown in the richest portion. The space between is suitable for Cauli- flowers and Broccoli. In cottage gardens the Celery is frequently planted a row here and there, an arrange- ment eminently fitted for small gardens, more especially if Peas are sown on the ridges, as by that means they do not shade the other crops so much, whilst in some instances they form an agreeable screen when far enough apart. If ground that is to be occupied by Celery could have the trenches formed now, there is every chance of securing a crop on each side. Those who have not planted Cabbage could do so to the very edge. Cauli- flowers and Lettuce would come away before soil would be required for the Celery. Ground that is now occu- pied by Broccoli and %ales of sorts will come in for later Celery or later Potatoes. The latter are planted by making an opening for each set with the spade in the space between each plant, and when the green crop is cleared away the ground is forked between the rows so as to get it into a fit state to earth the Potatoes with. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Clematis may now be pruned, by shortening the present years growth, within a short distance of its starting point. Our rule is to cut out all weak shoots within an eye or two of the previous year's growth, and unless there is much space to cover; all others are reduced to less than six eyes. Growing several feet in a year as these plants do from every bud, it is evident that they would become crowded if not severely thinned. Dielytra Spectabilis—the roots of which -are pierfeetly hardy, but its premature growth at this time subjects it to be nipped by frosts—is such an attractive object • when in bloom that every effort should be made to protect the young growth from in- jury in that direction.' If three or four wires or pliable Weis are bent over,to form support for a piece of sack- ing or some other fabric that might be thrown over them at night and moved in the clay, the plants would be per. safe. . 'FEB WINDOW.—The Dielytra makes an excellent win- dow plant, and the plants for this purpose should be lifted and potted anytime from November to the middle of February. They may then be plunged in ashes, and ifs soon as there are signs of growth moved into and placed in the window. Here they must be supplied with plenty of water till they have done flowering, and the leaves begin to turn yellow. After the end of May the plants may be stood outside and again plunged in ashes to prevent them blowing over and to avoid fre- quent watering. ' When all the top is quite dead it may be okayed and the siisface of the pot covered with an inch or two of ashes, and remain so till it starts to grow in February, when all the loose soil should be moved from the surface and replaced by a rich top dressing. Stimulants are best applied when the plant is half grown and after it has done flowering, for at this part of its ,oareer the plant is preparing itself for the campaign of the following year. Another plant milch neglected, is the Monthly rose or Fairy Roses as some call them. They are as easily grown as the Geranium, providing they are kept free from greenfly, which is easily done by 'fumigating with tobacco paper or tobacco itself. They flourish in rich loamy soil with a sprinkling of sand. The best time to prune them is about Midsummer, by oving all weakly growth. After the plants have dowered they are best out of doors, and in dry weather they must be well supplied with water.

PERSECUTION OF PROTESTANTS.—DetaiIs of perse.cutions of native Protestants in the island of Mate, one of the Loyalty group, show that French officials in that island, acting, it would seem, under the authority of the Governor of New Caledonia, had imprisoned several native teachers, and, it is alleged, treated them with great cruelty. A pain- ful account of these occurrences having been sent to Mr. A. McArthur, M.P., by a correspondent in the Pacific, he has addressed a letter on the subject to the directors of the French Protestant Missionary Society, in the belief that if proper representations are made to the French Government they will direct the Governor of New Caledonia to protect the persecuted natives. THE PRINCE OF WALES AND THE COLONIES.—The Prince of Wales presided on Monday evening at a meeting of the Royal Colonial Institute in London. Mr. Frederick Napier Broome read a paper on Western Australia. The Prince of Wales said everything connected with our colonies, and eepecially with Australia, could not fail to be of deep In- terest to the English people. Facts concerning these die- tant colonies should he brought prominently before them. Anything which would tend to unite the interests of the mother country and her colonies must always be of import- ance to Englishmen. The manner in which they had offered to assist England in a distant land showed that they Clung to the mother country.
SEASONABLE 'HINTS.

DYNAMITE FIRED FROM A CANON.—TERRIBLE EFFECTS. —Some remarkable experiments have just taken Diane in America with projectiles charged with dynamite, but dis- charged from the gun by gunpowder in the usual manner. An elastic buffer prevents a premature explosion of the projectile itself. At a range of 1,000 yards several six- inch shells, each chargea with 111 b of nitro-glycerine of 95 per cent purity, were fired at a -target, which consisted of the solid (trap) rock. A single shell dislodged many tons of rock, and made a cavity 25ft in diameter and eft deep, while the fragments were scattered over a distance of half a mile. The Russian Minister and the attach6l of the Ger- man, French, and Italian Ministers were present and wit- nessed the experiments.

Uncleanliness about the fowls, their quarters. or their runs is a sure cause of disease. Uncleanliness generates vermin, and vermin sap the foundations of health. Hens will not lay well or thrive well if infected with lice, nor will they, if they can avoid it, roost in filthy places and inhale the noxious gases which emanate from their ac- cumulaod droppings. Badly ventilated fovrlhouses and the absence of light and sun exert a powerful influence for evil on the health of fowls, and neglect of attention to cleanliness, food, and ventilation are a certain cause of ill-success in the poultry yard.

MEETING OF THE TORT PART.—On Monday a private conference of the Conservative members of th 3 House of Commons was held at the Carlton Club. Sir Stafford Northeote presided, and nearly 150 members wete present, in addition to the Marquis of Nalisbury, who attended as one of the negotiators in the recent agreement between the leaders of both political parties regarding the Seats Bill. The meeting was summoned mainly in order that an understanding might be arrived at with regard to such lead- ing features of that measure as have not already been dealt with in Parliament—an understanding considered especially necessary in view of the fact that most 0 the Conservative members, including several cccupants of the flout Opposi- tion bench, voted against Sir Stafford Northcote on Friday night in the division upon Aid. Fowler's proposal to retain four members for the city of London. During the discussion stress was laid upon the fact that only two or three Con- servative members followed their leader on that occasion, although the right hon. baronet's course was taken in accor- dance with an agreement which Lord Salisbury and himself had deliberately entered into with regard tc the Redistribu- tion Bill. Sir Robert Peel, Mr Chaplain, and other gentle- men spoke in justification of their vote. Compla.int was made that the leaders had not taken their party into their confidenoe as to the salient and essential featurca of the agreement which had been entered into with the Govern- ment, several speakers expressing their objection tinder the circumstances to surrendering their independent judgmeat. It was urged that some indication should be given to the points which were considered vital. In respanse, this was done as far as possible with respect to the remaining Clauses, and. at the same time an appeal was made to mem- bers to place a loyal confidence in their leaders, whose chief desire was to promote the welfare of the party. At the close of the proceedings those present were expressly urged to treat the business as confidential, and net to disclose what had taken place. MRS. S. A. - It is repoited that in one of the Southern counties the farmers intend to sow wheat extensively, instead of barley or oats, on the chance of war prices. Mr. Robert Brio, Great Smeaton, Northallorton, has bought for export' to America a lot of nine yearling Shorthorn bulls* fibril the herd at Bettie, Banff. The bulls are to be sent to Mr. J. J. Hill, St. Paul,.Minnesota, - • Mr. William Fort, of Cross Roads, Keighley, purchased the stout and powerful three-year-old Lincoln 3,806 at the Shire Horse Show in London last' week. Lincoln must be a most useful sire for the hilly: districts of Yorkshire.;-Hei was bred in Wiltshire, and shown by Mr. Godding, sold to Mr. Forshaw, who re-sold him to the present owner. -, • Professor Roberts considers corn the best crop for an orchard. Other crops draw upon the soil for food and moisture just at the time the young trees need nouri- ment most, whereas corn makes its demands upon the soil later in the season, at the proper time to check the too rapid growth of the young tree, making it hardy and vigorous for the winter. The Duke of Sutherland has set another example to Highland proprietors. He has intimated to the Crofter tenants that he will give about 15,000 acres of sheep- farm in Ardmadale, to be divided into small farms among those of the Crofters who have the enterprise and the means to take them. The portion of land selected for the purpose is an admirable blending of arable and reclaimable land, along with pasture. TER BATTLIE or TES SEPARATORS.-.-At the recent agricultural exhibition in Paris, the two :rival centri- fugal separators which caused such an amount of dis- cussion at the late London Dairy Show, once more came into competition. At the latter show the Laval won the first prize, the second going to the Danish. At the Paris Shovrthe positions have been reversed, the Danish winning first prize and gold medil, the Laval, second prize and silver medal. CASTRATION.—This operation should be performed when the calveS are-from six to eight weeks old, espe- cially if the calves are of pure breed. If left till as many months of age, they are apt to grow coarse and Ishaggy about the head, which tells against their value as steers. If the calves are intended for "baby beef," it is better to have them castrated at the proper age, than left to get coarse, of inferior quality, and troublesome. Fat male lambs are better for the operation, and their flesh is improved by it.—Midland Farmer. BRITISH DAIRY FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.—The annual report of this association save :—Sinoe the general meet- ing, in June last, the membership has been increased by the election of 134 noblemen and gentlemen, making a total of 465 now on the books. The Council are exceed- ingly desirous that this number should be materially in- creased, in order to enable them to take more active steps for the promotion of British dairying. Hitherto their efforts have been in a large measure, directed to the show which has been. annually held at the Agricultural Hall, the smallness of the funds at their disposal having prevented them from more fully developing the aims of the association. They earnestly believe that the time has nowiarrived when the society' scapacity for useful- ness will be recognised by a large section of agricul- turists who are practically interested in the dairy in- dustry, and that, therefore, the present year will witness a large accession of members. _

Corre- spondent describes a walk in North Lancashire in the month of February, which he says gives one an idea of how agriculturists hereabouts are progressing in these bad times. Passing over the hill districts, he says:— These who yet persevere in ploughing in this far-away district lusually divide their cropping as follows :—(1) Oats out of ley; (2) turnips, a few rows of rnangolds and potatoes; and (3) oats with seeds—quantity varying from three acres to eight or 10, accordiug to the size of the holding. On our return, in climbing out of the val- ley by a different route, and over a much poorer common than the one we crossed in going, we found the Herd- wick sheep here, as well as those elsewhere, looking very well and healthy. The frost in this district has not been severe enough to do harm, while the snow has not lain long enough to stop the supply of food. Every breed of sheep to their district. Any other pure-bred breed of sheep having to find their entire supply of food on these commons would stand a poor chance of existing long. AsourroN IN DAIRY Cows.—There ark says a corre- spondent of a contemporary, many complaints of pre- mature calving of dairy cows in the south of Ireland at present, several farmers suffering to a large extent by i it. It seems to be now pretty well established that the prin- cipal cause of this s ergot in the grasses. Not being an authority on fungi, I would have said that such a dry season as we have had would have been rather against the ergot theory; but a scientific friend re- marked to me the other day that a dry summer after a wet one was most favourable to the growth of ergot and all kinds of fungus, and he added, Have you not ob- served the large crop of mushrooms we had: last autumn?" I had one case myself, but immediately separated the cow from the others, whitewashed the stall, and used disinfectants, and by this means prevented its spreading, as I believe there is no doubt but serious results follow the neglect of these precautions: I have been from time to time much troubled with abortion in my dairy herd, and one year had eight cases out of 25 cows. I could never trace the cause—it has always been a mystery; but I am bound to say I have frequently discovered ih my fields numbers of specimens of ergotted grasses.
Public Analysts have submitted CIDBURy'S Cocoa to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus. taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

Ductasia A GAY Lornaaro.—At Shirley, on Monday morning, a curioas scene was witnesses, in which a fascina- ting young commercial traveler named Cotterill, was rath.r roughly need at the hands of an indignant Birmingham tradesman, named Turner, whose wife he had eloped with Cotterill and the woman had been staving at the Saracen's Head, a hotel in the village, since Saturday, and hearing of their whereabouts, Turner, with four friends, repaired there early yesterday morning. They found Come!' just as he was about to drive away in a gig. Dragging him from the vehicle, they promptly transferred him into a horsetrough in front of the hotel. Buckets of water were soused over him, and finishing with a bucket of pigevash, his tormentors let him free and chased their victim over several fields, be- labouring him with sticks freely, he being unable to offer the slightest resistance. At length he was allowed to regain the trap from which he had bean dragged, and made off as fast as he could—a truly pitiable object. His fair inamorata, whom he had left in bed, was meanwhile interviewed by her husband.

THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL. The Rouse again went into committee on the Redistribu- tion of Seats Bill -On clause 8 Mr iterenee moved an amend- ment the object of which was to divide boroughs returning only two members as well as places returning more than two tnembers, in order to carry oat further the principle of single-member constitrrenties.—Sir C. DUKE said person- ally he was in [avoer of single-member districts, but the general principle of the bill was to interfere as little as pos- sible with the existing iniMrests of uaiddleisized mutat:ten- cies, and by that principle the Government must abide. The Gevernment had 'lO &eke to adhere rigidly to the letter of the bill, and woald be -reedy to meet the general wishes of the House. He thought there could be no doubt that those constituencies which did not receive an increase of mem- bers did set desire to be divided into parts.—Sir S. Noerw- COTE wished to reendve an impression that the Conservative party were opposed to single-member districts. They were really anxious to introduce such districts as likely to se- cur.) the represedtation of minorities. The Government accepted the principle, but only as a compromise, as it was doubtful how far it would be acceptable in the country. There had Linea than beim a consider Ale change in public feeling, but as the Government called upon the House to adhere to the lines of the bill he should undoubtedly do so. —Mr. GLADSTONE remarked that unless there was some much stronger reason given for a change it was not desir- able to interfere with the historical unity and common life of towns that for a long time had existed as communities underour present system.—Upon a division the amendment was rejected by 253 to 44.—A eicassion took place upon the' one man one vote" principle.—On clause 27, ‘which disfranchises for ever certain persons found guilty of cor- rupt practices at the lost election, Mr. RAINES moved to leave out the words 'for ever," and to render the person named' incapable of voting dnring a period of seven years afteethe presentation of the Commissioner's report regard- ingthe elections.—There was considerable ditcussion, and it. was ultimately agreed to strike out the words "for steer " and to insert "for a peried of seven years." The ether 'clauses of the bill haring been agreed to, the ecm- mittee proceeded to consider the proposed new clauses "Mr. HENRY TOLLEMACIIE appealed to the Committee to ex- punge the clause. DILRE, in answer to Mr. Monk, said it was not necessary to reprint the Bill, as no amendments of any importance had been made. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock. 411211 Y • EXPENDITIJIM—The CilawCFMtert of the Ex CHEQUER stated that it was not intended to move for the appointment of a committee to inquire into army and navy expenditure during tho present session while the depart- ments were overwhelmed • with work, but there seemed no reason why an inquiry into the civil expenditure should not take place, and be intimated that he should renew his notice on the subject.—Mr. W. H. SISRT6 suggested the ap- pointment of a mixed committee which should include a number of experts to deal with the important questions in- volved in army and navy expenditure, mad Mr. CsrumEss promised to communicate with his colleagues on the sub- ject. Tux SEATS BILL —The greater part of the afternoon was devoted to the consideration in Committee 61 the -schedules to the Redistribution Bill. Proposals to strike out Beau- marts and Berwick from the disfranchising schedule were rejected.—Sir R. PEEL asked that Tamwerth, which was illustrous in political annals, might be permitted to give the name to one of the divisions of either Warwickshire or Staff ,rdshire, and Sir C. DrucE promised to give careful consideration to the suzgestion.—There was a long discus- sion upon the proposal of the Government as to the group- ing of the Scotch burghs. EGYPTIAN FINANCE.

The Crrawcarlo-n-e-f the Excuser:run, in explaining what had been done with respect to Egyptian finance, said the in- ternational agreement arrived at consisted of a declaration signed by the Great Powers and Turkey, covering a Con- vention by the same Powers, arid a project or decree to be issued by the Khedive. The Convention had been signed, and the Khedive had undertaken toeign the decree. As the result of discussions occupying months the Powers agreed to fix the normal administrative erpenditure of Egypt at £5,237,000 a year, subject to certain adjustments, and in that item was contained the sum of £200,000 a year as the maximum charge for the army of occupation in Egypt. It was agreed also that the sum to be raised now on loan should be £9,000,000 sterling, that the system of taxation should be extended to foreigners, and that two years should be given during which England should make an exhaus- tive inquiry as to the revenues of Egypt during those two years. The English proposals as te the abatement of the interest on the bonds have been agreed to to the extent that there is to be a redaction of -s.per cent on all the coupons of the bonds, and a reduction of per cent on the interest of the Suez Canal shares. If at the end of two years a continued reduction from the coupons is necessary, the Khedive is to summon an International Commission, which is to renew the general inquiry as to Egyptian finance. The loan is to be the subject of an in- ternational guarantee on the model of the•Aoglo-French guarantee of the Turkish loan in 1855. which was purely financial. The guarantee is of the annual-sum of £315,000 until the whole loan is paid off, and is to be the first charge on the revenues assigned by the debt and received by the Caisse. There is to be a sinking fund only applicable to the present loan, and that fund may be augmented to the extent of 1 per cent out of any future surplus on the general, revenue of the country. As to be free use of the Suez Canal, the Powers, taking the Granvillecircular of January. 1883 as a basis, have agreed that the details should be re- ported upon by the delegates meeting in Paris before the end of this month, with a view to an International Act be- ing agreed upon by all the Powers.—Mr. NOWOOD : Will any arrangement about the Suez Canal be submittal to this House P—The CniNcEmort of the EXCIIHRCER : sir, it is not a financial arrangement.— The subject then dropped.. _ _ _
The other business was disposed of, and the House ad- journed at six o'clock,_
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Taussper.

MiscguarrEons.—ln the absence of the Lord Chancellor the Earl of Redesdale took his seat on the woolsack in the House of Lords —The second reading of the Foisons Bill was moved by Lord CMILINGFORD, who expf tined that it proposed to take the whole subjet of poisons out of the Pharmacy Act and give to P. e Privy Council power to regu- late the sale of poisons.—The bill was read a second time without a division. The Earl of WEsvess, who said he had received a telegram from the Duke of Westminster urging him to press for the equip- ment and organisation of volunteers, postponed his motion with regard to the want of organisation of the auxiliary forces until after Easter.—The Duke of MauLiso,uoudit moved that any arrangement with the Powers, either politi- cal or financial, which might tend;to impair or dimimish the infuence of England in the administration of the affairs of Egypt would be unacceptable to the House.—Earl G.g.tat- lux declined to give any reply to the motion, which was one of censure of a hypothetical character, and said it was most unreasonable to propose a vote of censure until the papers were in their Lordships' hands.—The Marquis of SAldsgtaiX had beard with dismay that a discussion on the subject was to take place in the House ot Commons imme- diately. As this was one of the most momentous questions which had occupied the attention of Parliament for many years, he trusted the Government would not press for the decision of Parliament at too early a period.—l he Duke of Manutonocan than withdrew his motion. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes after six o'clock. LIOUCE OF COMNlONS.—Thrmsnay.

The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. FINANCES OF EGTlg.—The PRIME MINISTER announced that the House would adjourn for the Easter recess on Tuesday in Passfot3 Week, and meet again on Thursday, the 9th April, at the some time intimating that there would be a longer holiday at Whitsuntide.—Sir STAFFORD NORTE- COTE asked that the discassion.on the finances of Egypt might be put off until after the holidays.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that the proceedings of the House of Commons on the subject would he looked to by the other States, and he wag afraid that any serious postponement of a decision would lead to considerable farther delay. He was willing to postpone the discussion to the Monday in Passion Week, which would give a week for the consideration of the papers, but as at present advised he could not give a pledge to a postponement until after Easter. suypi,r.—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply on the Army Estimates several interesting military topics ware discussed. Mr. W. li. 6stlrs called attention to the unsatisfactory condition of our marine defences, and was informed by Lord Henrisrerrow that provision was made in the estimates for the formation of a coast corps of Royal Engineers upon the same principle as the Coast Corps of the Royal Artillery, and that the duty of the new corps would be to take charge of and superintend the submarine and mining defences of important stations, and also the training, drill- ing, and recruiting, of militia and volunteer submarine min- ing companies, Lie added that an exPenditnte ot two sod

a half millions would be necessary before the defencerof the great military ports at home and abroad could be considered completely satisfactory. The time when by a great effort they ought to cemplete the armament of these portreeequired great coesideration.—Colonel STANLEY contended that , should be a settled system of defen: :en; dOwn, and the Materiel for cArf:,t; should be at hand or in a state of ef6clency. . ARMY ESTIMATES....-LOrd TIARTINGTON made his state- ment upon the Army Estimates, remarking that owing to events in Egypt the estimates were of a provisional charac- ter, and that the fall demands that would have to be made could not be known until the vote of credit for Egypt was asked for. The estimates, he said, provided, in addition to the ordivary home and colonial departments, for aeoccupy- ing force of 6,000 men in Lower Egypt, loran estimated ex- penditure of half a million on the Bechuenaland expedition, but nothing either for the Nile expedition, the Suakim ex- pedition, or the Suaklm-Berber railway. The original es-i- -mates amounted to £15,930,600. In August a vote of credit was Obtained for £300,000 for the Nile expedition and in the autumns further supplementary estimate of 1,975,000 for the Nile and Bechuanaland expeditions. Since the es- timates bad been laid on the table a supplementary esti- mate for the present year of £942,000 had been asked for, making in all £2,917,000 in addition to the normal estimates, making a total for the military services of £18,847,600. The amount of the pre- sent estimate was £11,320,700 for the ordinary services of the year, an increase of £1,120,000. Referring to the state of the army, the noble Marquis said the number of effec- tives on January 1, 1884, was 173,529, and on January 1, 1885, it was 181,000, or an increase of about 7,500 men. The rate of recruiting has gone on, and on the Ist of March last there were in the army 184,209 effectives. He men- tioned that at the present time there were in Egypt and the Baudan twenty and a half battalions, numbering 16,400 men, or according to the lag return 15,900 effectives. Pro- ceeding with his statement, Lord Hartington said the loss in the army by death, invaliding, an discherge or desertion was less than at any time during the last 21 years. In the last year the first-class army reserve had increased by 4,700 men, bringing its total number up to to 39,244% and the total fighting strength of the army was now 40,000 in ex- cess of what it was ten years age.—Progress was afterwards reperted.

LAKE Dwattisios.—The British Society of Antiquaries, I London, have just made a grant of money for the pur- pose of excavating another of the lake dwellings at Ul- rome. The first of these dwellings was discovered in 1880 by Mr. Thomas Boynton, of Uirorne Grange, who has been carrying on excavations to the present time. The discovery has,cansed lunch ,interest in the scientific circle, and the work of -laying bare another of these abodes of the ancient 'thy:tilers in the Holderness eduntry will be watched with: much interest, especially as the one it is proposed to excavate is of much greater extent than the previous one. The grant from this important society has been secured mainly through the exertions of the Rev. Canon GreenwelL the well-known anti- quarian, who has taken great interest in the discovery from the first. CAsiirestisu os. FisirEs.—A few weeks ago I opened the stomach of a cod-fish weighing 841bs. I found in it two full-grown herrings, one large Whiting, one codling, seven flounders, ode small sole, and one small skate, all newly swallowed. From the mouth of the whiting a large live world issued. Besides these were half- digested temente of other fish, chiefly flounders. VI the large-mouthed fishes are curiously voracious' and usually cannibals. I have 'seen ' a small eel 'swallow a still smaller eel, head first, the tail hill of the swallowed fish projecting from the mouth of-the swallower, and moving for some hours. The swallowing thenceforth proceeded very slowly, evidently Recording to the rate of digestion of the part that had reaclaed.the stomach, as some days elapsed before the end of the tail of the swallowed fish disappeared. To show the mouth capacity of some fishes, take two John Dous of equal size; open the mouth of one to its full capacity, and it will be found large enough to take in the whole of the second fish.— Gentleman's Magazime. THE PRICE OF MR. HOLUM; HUNT'S GREAT PICTURE —lt having been stated by the Pall Mall Gazette that Mr. W. Holman Hunt was asking £20,000 for his new picture of "The Triumph of ' the Innocents," Mr. Hunt writes—" I am reminded of a strong reason for correct- ing this misstatement. The sum I once offered the painting at was considerably short of this, although, indeed, had the amount named been paid me, so great has been the expense in executing the work, owing mainly, it is true, to exceptional circumstances, that the liberal sum published would scarcely, pay me the com- monest journeyman's wages. I would not at this time undertake to deliver the picture for even twice the money named. The enly natural patrons of works for me, as I follow my art, with costly and unceasing effort to procure thorough Oriental truth for Biblical subjects, are the people. On previous occasions the interest in the result of my study in Syria itself of the nature still there—which best perpetuates the character of the nation from which we get our religion—has been ade- quately declared by the public, or I should not have been able to persevere in myeourse. It is to them I now look for recognition more than to any single individual, be he ever so much a millionaire or an enterprising middleman."

THE Peeve/47.1mi or Thrnnomonis.—The report for 1884 of Mr. Ernest Batt, the veterinary officer of the Brown Institution, shows that the work of the hospital has been efficiently carried on and highly appreciated by the owners of animals; 222 in-patients and 3,269 out- patients were treated during the year; the majority were horses and dogs. The fact of most general impor- tance was the occurrence of a series of cases of rabies during a short period towards the end- of the year; the outbreak has, however, apparently subsided. Dr. Bur- den Sanderson, when professor superintendent, suggested that the leading symptoms of rabies should be printed on the back of dog licensee; some permanent official in the Inland Revenue Department probably resisted this innovation. The suggestionl if brought to the notice of the present enlightened President of the Local Govern- ment will, it may be hoped, meet with a better fate; the cost of carrying it out ought not to _exceed a few, shil- lings a year, A great deal of .ignorance intdoubtedlY exists with regard to the symptoms of rabies, of the "dumb" form especially, yet the recognition of the disease in its early stage, before the dog has become ferocious and helpless, is of the greatest importance. If the first cases were recognised in their earliest stages, it would be comparatively easy to stamp out a commencing epidemic.—British Medical Journal. ELECTRIC LIGHT val.-norm DYNAHO6.—At Messrs. Blum- berg's offices, in Cannon-street, London on Monday, there was exhibited a new form of electric lighting, which bids fair to become very popular' inasmuch as the electricity is generated without any complications of dynamos, wires, and accumulators. A battery of very small size, say 6 by 4 by 2 inches, containing material for producing light equal to twenty to twenty-eve ,candles for ten or twelve hours can be concealed from view in the vase of an ordin- ary eolza-oil or pretroleum lamp, and in place of wick the lamp is fitted with a Swan or otherincandesent "burner." The llpttery is worked similarly to the ordinary galvanie batte.V. Thereare cells contaudng a solution of caustic potash in which are plates of zinc, connected with silver plates inserted in pockets of chloride of silver. The cur- rent of electricity which produces the light can be instan- taneously turned on and off at pleasure; and when turned off all galvanic action ceases. Thus, a light which, if continually burning, would last, say, ten hours, can be made to burn about five nights at two hours each: and so on; while a policeman's dark lantern can be kept in one's bedroom, and if only turned on for a second or so at a time, to see the hour,&c., may last for months with a minimum of attention. The question of cost has not yet been, arrived at so completely as to admit of definite commercial quotation for the lamps; but a combination is being formed to promote a company for working the patents. The rough - calculation is made that., m its' present stage, an electric light of about twenty-five can- dle power can be used at a cost (irrespective of prime cost of the apparatus) of three farthings to a penny an hour; but more information will doubtless be shortly afforded, and as a luxury a ready sale may reasonably be predicted, provided the materials to be used can be read- ily obtained, and a system of interchangeability of parts cad be introduced. For instance, it would be ,desirable that the silver plate with the chloride of silver thrown on to it by conversion could be exchangeable for a fresh plate ready for use. These points,homever, are matters of detail which can be left to business men to solve.• The invention is applicable to arc lighting as well as in- candescent burners, and the lamp lately experimentally used by the Thames police for lighting the river was also exhibited. This lamp is the size of a small" tail light "affixed to the end of the last carriage of a train, and the apparatus for generating the electricity was two boxes, each about 10 by 8 by 6 inches.

"THE ANGLO-RUSSIAN DISPUTE. ST. PETEASBEIRGI, MonnAr.—There is a rumour in circu- lation that direct communication has passed between the 'Queen and the Cz tr, which lam able to mention as a ru- mour only. To-day's Norse rremya remarks that the statement of Mr. Gladstone in the House of Commons has pat an end to the alarmist rumours of the last few days, and shows that the two Powers have at least agreed to respect the status quo without coming into collision on the Afghan Irontier, while a solution of the difficulty is being sought after by diplomatic negotiation—Tunes. TEHERAN, SIINDAY.—A. letter received here from Asia. bad, dated February 24th, states that extraordinary precau- tionary measures are being taken at Askabad in regard to strangers and their communication with the outside world. Troops and military stores are being sent daily t9wards Merv. Altogether 16,000 troops of all arms are spoken of as having been ordered to proceed to Merv.

BOXBra, FRIDAY.—t deputation of the Mussulman popu- lation have waited upon the Governor to express their hope that the Governthent would be firm in resisting Ruesian aggression upon Afghanistan. The Governor replied that it was the duty of the Government to resent any encrotch- ' merit upon the Afghan frontier, however powerful the I neighbour might be. The leader of the deputation assured I the Governor that England might rely upon the Mussul- mans of India to give her their utmost material and moral support. In a conversation with a distinguished General who was 1 advocating a plan of railway extension in Turkestan, the Cs tr uttered the following words, which at the present crisis are vested with the highest importance :—"I cannot conceive that any but the wildest dreamers can imagine for one instant that I have the intention of declaring war, seeing that no success of our areas would repay us for the sacrifice we should be called upon to make. The future of Russia in Asia," continued the Emperor. "is predestined to a glorious accomplishment by means of the irresistible march of civili- sation, and not by the employment of force." According to the Gaulois, the Cz tr, in replying to the letter of the German Emperor, says that the Afghan ques- tion has never threatened the peaoe of Europe. Awaiting its settlement, the Clear adds that Russia has come to a temporary agreement with England on the basis of the uti possidetis. The Pall Hall Gazette says that a satisfactory despatch has arrived from Sir E lwd. Thornton. M. Gists assures him that the Russian Government agrees that the tele- graphic assurances constitute au arrangement forbidding further advance. . . . . .

It is said that the instructions sent by the Russian Government on the sth inst. to General Komaroft cannot reach the Russian advanced posts until the 20th inst. The Afghan outposts at Penideh, however, may have already received the British advice. FRANCE.—THE CHINESE HOSTILITIES.—SEARCH _ OF ANOTEIER I3RITISh VESSEL.

SAARBRITECK, WEDNESDAY, 7 P.M explosion of fire. damp occurred in the Camphansen coal mine, near DM- welter, shortly before one o'clock this morning. Of 219 miners who descended the shaft for the night shift 30 only are reported to be saved, this number iacluding 16 who had left the mine before the explosion occurred. The main shaft fell in after the explosion, and the ventilating apparatus was destroyed. Every effort is being made to save the men in the pit, but there seems little hope of success, as the workings are blocked in every direction. Up to the pre- sent hour 92 badies have been brought to the pit's mouth. SLARBRUEC74 , TEMISDAY.—Up to three o'clock this afternoon 51 miners had been rescued alive from the Camp- bausen pit in which the explosion occurred, yesterday, and 137 bodies bad been brought to the surface.

ARREST OF ZEBEHR PASHA AND HIS SON.-REPORTED FALL OF KAS- SALA. CAIRO. SUNDLY.—Z.Ibehr Pasha was arrested at four o'clock yesterday afternoon. He was taken at his house in Tenoosi, near Alexandria, and was conveyed at once on board her Majesty's ship Iris. which left for Malta with him on board this afternoon. I learn that his arrest is in conse- quence of the receipt of information that General Bracken- bury's column found among the enemy's effects some com- promising correspondence from him. Preparations have been quietly going on for this event for some days. Zebehr's house has been searched for compromising does- manta, and his son has been arrested. The English military authorities have throughout acted in this matter entirely upon their own responsibility. ALEXANDRIA, SONDAY.—Zebehr Pasha's son and three other persons have been arrested at Cairo, and were brought here in custody this morning. Many seizures of papers have been made. Cetao, Nlortnev.—The main subject of discussion is the arrest of Zebehr Pasha, awl whatever may be its ultimate resalt, it is undoubted that it has produced an immediate and wholesome effect. It cannot by too strongly pointed Out that much of the opposition incurred has been due to our exaggerated deference to the susceptibilities of natives and foreigners, which has been entirely misunderstood. The latest news of the state of affairs at Kassala was re- ceived here from Suakirn last night. The news is dated February 16th, at which time the place had not been taken. I A rumour was current at Saakim that Kassala had been cap- tured, but at present there is no confirmation et the report. I Nothing has been heard here of a massacre of the garrison. Curio, TIIESDAY.—Cherif Pasha, Abdul Rahman Pasha,l and ~a number of others have personally waited upon the I Khedive, protesting against the arrest of Zebehr Pasha by British authorities as neing altogether unwarrantable. The supplicants obtained little satisfaction. _ _

Sraxim, Senrunay.—The natives yesterday continued their tactics of harassing our sentries. In the skirmishes which took place in the different camps two English soldiers were wounded. It is believed, however, that the assailants lost heavily. The 20th Hussars and the 28th Bengal have arrived. News from Kassala has been received, dated Mar. let. The garrison were then still holding cut. STMEIIf, SIINDAY.—A heavy fire was kept up in all parts of the camp last night between the garrison and the rebels. No casualties occurred on our side. Native spies keep the British authorities well informed of Osman Digina's move- ments. General Graham's leg is now completely healed, but he is still somewhat lame.

STUMM, MOMDAY.—AII the cavalry paraded this morning, including the Indian contingent, who were made the subject of special commendation. Several of the camps have been shifted to-day, including the Guards, to render them more secure against night attacks. Suextra, WEDNESDAY.—A general advance on Tami is expected to be mide on Friday morning. A spy has arri- ved here from Assidnt, and. reports that the Anwar tribe is ready to join the British.

THE CAMP AT KORTI. KOESTI. THUIISDAY.—Lord Wolseley, with bis Staff, re- turned here at noon to-day from Ahu. Dom, after inspecting the camp. The troops generally are in good h-alth, few cases of sickness baing reported. The desert ~r..bs state that a new Afandi has appeared in Kordofan, but title cre- dence is given to the story here. General Greaten and Major Kitchener leave here to-morrow, the latter to join the Staff of General Wood, whose headquarters are at Debbeh. LORD WOLSELEY SUGGESTED AS

GOVERNOR-GENERAL. The Central News correspondent at Cairo telegraphs on Monday night that the British authorities there urge that Lord Wolseley should be made Governor-General of the Sondan, in place of the late General Gordon, in order to convince the natives that England will not abandon the Soudan until a stable Government has been instituted. Lord Wolseley strongly approves of the plan, and the necessity of adopting it has been urged upon the Horne Government. Her Majesty's Ministers appear, however, averse to this step, alleging that It might pledge them to prolong the oc- cupation of the Soudan by England. Sir Evelyn Baring cordially endorses the proposed appointment. REVOLT AGAINST THE

ROOTS, SATURDAY.-A native from Omdurman reports that the Mandi's uncle has been killed in a rebellion in Kordofan, and that preparations are being made to send a kody of men there. Darfour is also hostile to the Mandi. When Khartoum was taken all the Europeans and Egyptians were killed, and also the runs of Kasin el Moos. The chil- dren were spared. The army at Omdurman was small, troopehad been sent down the river, some of whom were recalled and despatched to quell the disturbance in Kordo- fan. On the way back the spy beard that the Hassaniyeh were going to raid on the Hawawi, who were preparing to resist them. Since the fall of Khartoum the camp had been near Fort Omdurman. Much illness prevailed among the men in the rebel camp. The Mandi was much displeased with Ids followers at their having killed General Gordon, as he wished to question him as to the treasures which he is convinced are hidden somewhere. The price of grain at Kkartoum is enormous. The Mabdi tells his men that they will next be wanted to fight the rebels at Kordofan, not the English, who will be killed by the heat. DJEDDAII, Sernmaay.—lntelligence received here slaVs that fresh proclamations from the Mandi have been distri- buted in Yemen and other parts of Arabia.

SUAKIM. SUAKIM, THURSDAY, 12-3,5 Ir.—General Graham has replied to Osman Digma's menacing letter. The General declares that the English respect all religions, and desire to maintain friendly relations with all the Arab tribes. He advises the sheikhs to submit without delay, and rely on the mercy of Eegland; and he thr.atens if they refuse sub- mission to destroy their followers, flocks, and property.

The following telegram has been sent by Lieutenant- General Sir G. Graham to Lord Wolseley, dated Suakim, Thursday, 6-40 pin. :—" I carried out reconnaissance to Elasheen this morning with Cavalry Brigade and Mounted Infantry. Infantry of Indian contingent moved out about four miles In support. Enemy retired in front of us, evac- uating village of Hasheen and making far the mountains. Slight opposition offered by isolated parties. Left replies to Osman Digma's letter on posts. Force back in camp 12-30. Weun4ed, Lieutenant J. R. K. Birch, Mounted In- fantry, who behaved very gallantly. Shall form entrench- ments near Hasheen to-morrow morning. Garrison em- ployed, East surrey Regiment. _

_ INSPECTION AT KORTI. Komi, FRIDAY.—Lord Wolselev inspected the force under Major-General Darner at the Tani camp to-day. The camp is two miles north of Ambukol, on high ground. During the week 10 deaths have occurred in the camp at Korti Iron enteric fever. A letter from Berber has been re- ceived by Ihe Intelligence Department stating that many sympathise with the Khedive's Government, and state that the good behaviour of the British troops has produced a deep impression. Respecting Mahomed El Khur, his army is now dispersed, some at Metammeh and some at Abh Amed. The report of the Mandi having a great army is false ; the rebel army at Berber is 3,400 men. They have 7,000 Reroingtons—many of which are ueeless—aed four guns, one of them being useless. The letter concludes : " Fear not the power of the rebels." KORTI, FRIDAY 6-30 P M.—lntelligence has been received here that Mahomet El Kheir, the Emir, and the dervishes who had co.ne to Aka Amed to reinforce the garrison have returned again to Berber. It is also stated that the inhabit- ants of Berber who some time, since had crossed the Nile with the object of opposing the advance of our troops along the left bank of the river have again re- turned to Berber. Some natives entered the cemetery herr last night, and tore down and broke the crosses erected ovee the graves.

KORM SUNDAY.—General Sir Evelyn Wood's column arrived to-day from Gakdnl. The troops succeeded in bring- ing away all the stores and ammunition and deposited at the different wells in the desert. Some small pirties of robbers, who hovered round the column on its way to Ciak- dul, ceased following it after leaving Howeiyatt. Surgeon Bradshaw died here to-day of enteric fever. Koren, TVESDAL—Lord Wolseley will proceed shortly to inspect the camp at Abu Dom, near Merawi. General Grenfell is leaving here to inspect the line of communica- tions as far as Assiout. The General will assume the com- mand of the Egyptian army at the end of March. General Sir Evelyn Wood will command the troops quartered be- tween Merawi and Dongola. The Naval Brigade has been divided into four sections, stationed at different camps, under the respective commands of Lieutenants AWN-, Reed,- Montgomerie, and Hardy. Lord Charles Beresford will rejoin the staff of Lord Wolseley. CAIRO, WsottEsnev.—Nothing is known here to confirm the statement published its London on the afternoon of the 17th inst. asserting that a proposal had been mooted for appointing Lord IVdlseley to the post of Govemor-Geueral of the Soudan, in the place of the late General Gordon.

Following the example set by the cotton spinners of Sowerby Bridge, Ripponden, and Crag g Vale, the cot- ton spinners of West Vale and Greetland are this week reducing the working time to four days a week. SAD BOATING ACantanarY.—A distressing accident occur* red on the Thames at London Bridge on Sunday evening. Six young men and four young woqaen were proceeding down the river in a small boat, which was;capsixed through the femiles leaving their seats on meeting a little rough water. Two sailors and a lighterman put off in boats and rescued three of the men and one woman, but the other six were drowned.

He then left her lying in a .pooli Of blood, and gave himself up to the police. ; ' • I TRH Satvanorr ARMY.. —:The fourth anniversary of the opening of the Salvation Army campaign in France and Switzerland was celebrated by a large meeting on Monday in Exeter Hall, London. Miss Booth gave an account of the progress of the organisation on the continent, and said in Switzalaud the authorities still imposed heavy fines upon the adherents. In France conversions had been made, but there they had 60,000 priests opposed to them. BRUTAL 31VRDEL—A horrible tragedy is reported frost Woolwich, where one of the crew of no hired transport Kinserubo was found on Saturday night in a dying condi- tion, his face and head having been battered in a fearfel manner by some blunt weapon. A poker which was foun& in the vicinity, smeared with blood, was obviously the weapon with which the tragedy had been perpetrated. A I woman narnod Burch, and a man—Thomas Connor—have been arrested.

ENGLISH CRICKETERS ne AwaTrtatta.—The match be- tween Shaw's team and a representative Australian Eleven was, on Tuesday, at Sydney, unexpectedly brought to conclusion. The Australians, who, when play ceased ow Monday night, had eight wickets down for 303, were all out for 309. The Englishmen being thus 40 runs behin4 OS the first innings went in agsit),. but failed to make any stand, all the wickets falling for a total of 77. The 38,....rans required to win the match were mule up by the Austialisne with the loss of two wickets.

LIBERATED IRISH POLITICAL Patsowans —On Monday night Mr. O'Leary, ex-major-general in the Fenian move. merit. and associated with J. Stephens, arrived at Lime. rick accompanied by P. N. Fitzgerald, who was acquitted on the charge in connection with the Tubbercurry con- spiracy case. They were received at the railway termintur by a large crowd, and a procession, accompanied by twa bands' paraded the town. Addresses were presented ow arrival at the Wentworth Hotel, and Messrs. O'Leary and Fitz.rerald, after a few words in reply, were entertained at a banquet.

Tn7etcrv-wina LIVES LOST AT SEA.—The Liverpool ship Allegheny, it is feared, has foundered with all on board- -29 souls. The ship left Cirdief on January 9th with a cargo for Point de Gaffe. About two days after leaving port a series of terrible gales set in, during which many vessels either foundered or were seriously damaged. It was expected that the Allegheny would have been reported off Gibretar, or at any rate Port Said, on enter:ng the Suez Canal. This not having been the case, the vessel has been given up as lost with all en board. About a month ago a couple of life-buoys with the name "Allegheny,'. of Liver. pool," marked upon them, were washed ashore near the Mumbles. It was thee feared that some disaster had over- taken the vessel. When she left Cardiff she had a cargo of 2,700 tons of coals on board, and was under the command of Captain John Rea, of Bootle. SEATS AYD ELECTORAL AREAS.--A return of " Seats and Electoral Areas," just presented to Parliament, shows what are the constituencies which will still, under the Redistri- bution Bill, return more than one member each. None of them will return more than two. With the exception of the Universities of Oxford, Cambridge, and Dublin. they are :—ln England: Stockport, Derby, Devonport, Plymouth, Sunderland, Portsmouth, Southampton, Preston, Blackburn, Bolton, Oldham, Leicester, the City of Lon lon, Norwich, Northampton, Newcastle-on-Tyne, Bath, Ipswich, Bzighton, York, and Halifax. In Wales: Merthyr-Tydvil. Scot/and : Dundee. In Ireland : Cork. The order is the alphabetical order of the counties. All the coanties which return more than one member, all the boroughs which return more than two, and all the new boroughs are divided into single member constituencies. _ •

Prince Albert Victor was preEent —Mr Forster said their special object was to secure the permanent unison of the mother country with our self-governing colonies. Europe and England were too full, and to find an outlet we must Mater-die, and go to the temperate regions. We had done to, and 80 per temperateLenutthofAtthriecalo r gtihoen sEnogflisAhmrearciz,and 44 per cent were under British rule. He asked what nation would dare to attack a consolidated empire such as we Should present to the world. He combated a proposal for separation, ree marking that it was not in the interests of our Australian Colonies to be the object of amthion or intrigue of Conti- nental Governments. The War Office authorities hive decided to further align- ment the strength of the Railway Corps in the Sondakan with that object have called noon Lieutenant-Colonel ttj M. Palmer, commanding the Ist Newcastle-on-Tyne an Durham Engineer Volunteers, to furnish another detach , ment from that corps of locomotivi firemen and clea,ners; The detachment is being prepared, and will shortly pror ' ceed to Chatham for equipment: Depots having line btat talions abroad are in some CVO, by order of the War Office; calling upon the reserve of officers. This reserve numbers about 1,222 officers, viz, 15 generals, 37 lieutenant-generals, 65 major generals, 120 colonels, 346 majors, 602 captains, and 137 lieutenants. The following isstructions regarding enlistments for the brigades and battalions of militia which are embodied have been issued :--" The enlistrneut of militia recruits will be carried on as heretofore, men being posted to the embodied brigades or battalions as required, provided the establish- ment of the embodied brigade or battalion is not exceeded." The 62nd Army Signalling Class is ordered to assemble at Aldershot on Monday, and will be attended by about 50 officers and men from various stations. div.head: GORDON.
div.p: GORDON.
_ Miss Gordon, sister of Gtmeral Gordon, bas received Cie following letter from the Khedive _

Abdin Palace, Cairo, 24h February, IsBs. Madam,—Although I do not wish to intrude upon the great sorrow which has befallen you in the death of your distinguished brother, the late General Gordon Pasha, yet, as Egypt and myself have so mach reason to deplore his loss, I desire to convey to you my heartfelt sympathy in the terrible bereavement it has been God's will you should suffer. I cannot and words to express to you the respect and admiration with which your brother's ehnple faith and heroic courage have inspired me. The whole world resounds with the name of the Engliehman whose chivalrous nature afforded it for many years its brightest and most powerful example —an example which I believe will influence thousands of persons for good through all time. To a mere of General Gordon's character the disappointment of hops he deemed so near fruition and the sudden manner of his death were of little importance. In his own words, he left weariness for perfect peace. Our mourning for him is very true and real, as is our loss, but we have a sure hope that a life and death each as Gordon's are not extinguishable by what we cell death. I beg to renew to you, madam, the as- surance of my sincere sympathy and respectful cmdolence. MEHEMET TEWFIE.
