At the Borough Court, on Monday, some surprise was oe- cusioned by about thirty boye, of ages ranging from eight to fourteen years, being brought before the magistrates on charges of stone throwing in Mill-lane and Lovely-lane. The youngsters were marched in in single file, keeping good step. and were then formally charged. Amidst some laughter the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) informed the magistrates on the Bench that the defendants bad been taking part in a mimic Egyptian war, and that among them were Generals Roberts, Graham, and other officers. On Sunday, the Bth inst, they had two pitched battles, one in the afternoon and one in the evening, stones and sticks being freely used. These took place in the neighbourhood of Bank Quay, and there had also been a fight near the Horse and Jockey.—lnspector Spinks deposed to seeing a pitched battle between two gangs of boys, and several names haviag been secured a number of boys were taken to the police station, where they admitted the offenc. They said they were playing the Egyptian war. General Gordon and General Roberts were amongst them. (Laeghter.)—Mr. Fairclough : Which is the Mandi 2—lnspector Spinks : I don't exactly know. but he is amongst them somewhere. Backbones and Smith (two of the defendants) can tell you —Mr. Hunt poir.ting to one of the boys) : This is General Gordon —The Mayor : I suppose you are commanding officer ?—Defendant: No, sir, it is William Smith. (Laughter.) —The Mayor : What does he call himself 2—Defendant : General Wolseley. , (Laughter.)—The boy calling himself General Wolseley said that the Mill-lane boys had sticks and stones on the field ready to fight the Bostock-street boys. The latter took all the sticks and the others then commeeced throwing stone3.—The Clerk : Are you a Bostock-street boy 7—Yes. —Mr. Hunt : What is the name of the captain on the other side 2 That is the Mandi.—The Mayor : General Gordon, the Malidi, and you, General Wolseley, must be distinctly given to understand that this kind of warlike pro- ceeding will not be tolerated. If you want to fight you I had better go to Egypt, for we cannot allow you to fight in Warrington, and endanger your own lives and thosa of the public. I think the best thing to do would be to take you to the cells, and, notwithstanding your military distinction, to give you a sound flogging with the birch rod. That would not be very dignified for military people, but it will be tine fate that you will have to meet if you come here again on a charge of this sort. We shall make you experience the sensations of going to war. (Laughter.) We are sorry that your parents should be put to the distress of mind that they will be in coming here, but we cannot let you off, and have determined that as nit is the first offence we will only in- flict a penalty of is each. If you come again you may ex- pect to meet with the birch rod, and you may depend upon it you will be made to feel it very severely.—The fines were paid and the boys left the court with a crest-fallen appear- once.

Mr John Bagaley treated to more of such contumely, he , occupied the chair, and made a few remarks on temper. called a private meeting of the Conservative party, which was held on Monday at the Carlton Club. Lord SALISBURY was present, and supported his colleague in urging the necessity of playing properly the game of " follow your leader ;' but from the brief reports of the proceedings that have been made public, it would seem that the rebelli- ous spirits were not to be put down. It used to be the fashion for the Tories to be "kinder sarcastic" in describing the Liberals as a " happy family," because they had their differences as to the rate of progress that ought to be maintained. How will they like the phrase as applied to themselves—partic- ularly when their differences are seen to arise out of disorderly demands for scotching the wheels of the stage coach? Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE has no doubt his defects as a leader, and so has Lord SALISBURY, and so has every other man amongst them on the front opposition benches. Their great difficulty is that they are defective as a party; but if they are not altogether beyond tuition, they will learn that defection will not remedy their defects. They would have the people of this country believe that, as a party, they are much better able than the Liberals to manage the affairs of this nation; but they are not likely to carry conviction until they show some capacity for managing their own affairs. Their disorganisation is in some respects an advantage to the Government; but in others it is a disadvantage, for if the prevalent disorder continues it will be ap- parent that it is useless to make arrangements with leaders who cannot lead.

ADCS. Mawrtow or RUNCORN GUARDIANS.—Thursday next is the last day for nominating persons to serve upon the Board of Guardians for the Runcorn Union. The retiring members fer Runcorn are Messrs W Whittaker, W Handley, W Fisher, T Norman, and P Speakman; Weston: the Rev Canon Barclay and Mr E Aaron; Halton : the Rey J Lockwood. FORMATION OF A WIDNES BICYCLIST AND TRICYCLIST CLUD.—A number of " wheelmen " met at Unsworth's Dining Rooms on Wednesday, and decided to form a club under the above title. Mr E Knowles, of Irwell-street, was appointed secretary; Mr George Baker. treasurer; Mr W Handley, captain; Mr Wm Dixon, sub-captain; and a committee was selected. PROPERTY SALE AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Luke Holmes offered for sale, at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, a leasehold hair- dresser's shop, with two cottages adjoining, and situate in High-street, the property of the executors of the late John Hedgcock. The property, after some spirited bidding, was knocked down to Mrs. aleadowcroft for £270. Messrs. Day and Lake were the solicitors. THE BIRMINGHAM TRAGEDY.—Henry Kimberley, Was executed on Tuesday morning at Wilson Green Prison, for the murder of Mrs Palmer, by shooting her at the White Hart Hotel, Birmingham, last December. The condemned man walked steadily and without difficulty on to the drop, and, the lever being pulled, he seemed to die instantane- candy. The executioner was Berry, of Bradford. "ANT. AND THEIR Ways."—A lecture OD this subject WAS delivered in the Brunswick Wesleyan School on Wednes- day evening, under the auspices of the Mutual Improve- ment Society. The lecturer was Mr a Burns, who dealt with his subject Ins very instructive manner, and illustra- tions were thrown upon the screen by the oxy-hydrogen lantern of Mr Jlt Frith. Mr T Sirnister presided. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD EtEctioN.—At present there are no signs that this contest will ba fought in the spirit and determination which has been infused into it in former years. The only action taken by the rival associations so far has been the selection of the candidates, a list of which we published several weeks ago, but lively meetings may be expected before the voting papers are collected, three weeks hence. CONSERVATIVE ORGANISATION IN THE WIDNES DIVISION. —A meeting of Conservative gentlemen in the Widnes Division was held at the County Conservative Association, Liverpool, on Thursday, to consider the organisation of the party and select a candidate. The strictest secrecy was observed. It is rumoured that it was decided to bring for- ward Sir H Sullivan head of the firm of Messrs Sullivan and Co., of Widnes, if be would give his assent. NORTHWICH PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION.—The delegates appointed to represent Runcorn at the meeting of the General Liberal Council for the Division on Saturday met at Bethesda School on Wednesday, to discuss what course should be adapted, and to secure if possible united action. About 30 persons were appointed as delegates in place of those who had intimated their inability to be present st Northwich. Considerable discussion took place, but no de- finite course of action was decided upon, and each represent- ative will boat liberty to follow his own inclination in the suggestion of a candidate. WIDNES WESLEYAN CIRCUIT.—The quarterly meeting was held in Hartland Chapel, West Bank, on Monday even- ing, when the Rev J Hathersall was unanimously invited to labour in the oircuit for a third year, and the invitation to the Rev Robert Bardon to succeed the Rev R Harper was confirmed. During the evening reference was made to the valuable service rendered to the cause of Wesleyan Metho- dism by Mr Hartland for the past quarter of a century, and it was proposed to celebrate the jubilee of Widnes Metho- dism, which occurs this year, in some appropriate manner, but no definite action was resolved upon. NEW BUILDING SOCIETY AT RUNCORN.—A meeting con- vened by circular was held in the National Schools on Thursday, under the presidency of the Rev B. Edwards, when Mr J Connor delivered an address upon the advan- tages ef building societies conducted on the " ballot and sale " principle. It was decided to form a society to be called "The Runcorn and District Industrial Building Society," with Mr J E Meredith 89 secretary, Mr 0 Leak isolicitor, and Mr H White surveyor. The Rev R Edwards and Messrs E Imison, J Goodall, A Jordan, W Sutton, S H Dawson, and J K Digges. It was decided to ask MrJ Brun- drit, J.P., to act as president, and Messrs W Whittaker and .1 Meadowcroft as vice-presidents. PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE Co.—The 38th annual report of this gigantic society appears in our advertis- ing columns, and it will be seen from a peru- sal of it that it continues to make satisfac- tory progress. The total emote of the company have now reached the vast sum of £4,711,484, the increase for the past year being upwards of three quarters of a million sterling. As many as 11,828 new polices have been issuc during the year in the ordinary branch, assuming the sum of £1,359,361. The total number of policies in force in this branch ii 51,835. In the industrial branch the total num- ber of policies is over six millions, the premiums for the year amounting to £2,844,518. It is gratifying to note that this large business has been done with a reduction in ex- penditure of about two per cent on the premium income. The Prudential has evidently got a great hold upon the public, and it is likely to keep it. THE EMPLOYMENT OF RUNCORN MEN AT WIDNES.—Tho excitement with regard to the resolution of the Widnes Local Board, requesting the manufacturers to compel the Runcorn men in their employ to live in Widnes, or to cease to employ them, has fast died away. From the first, the general opinion was that the masters would altogether dia. I regard the request, but it is improbable that the resolution will be forwarded to them. Mr B Dutton has given notice I that at the neat meeting of the Board he will move that it be rescinded, and no doubt is entertained that he will suc- • ceed in his desire. We understand on good authority that the number of contractors across the footbridge from Run- I corn to Widnes, mentioned by Dr O'Keeffe, is greatly in excess of the actual fact. Four hundred contractors is the ' outside limit, and many of these are youths, apprenticed at 1 various places in Widnes. The return and single tickets I issued average about 50 per day, and these cannot by any means be classed as workmen's contracts. INSTITUTION OF A NEW JUVENILE TEMPLE AT WIDNES.—. A very interesting meeting took place in the Matins Tem- perance Hall, Simm's Cross, on Tuesday evening, the occa- sion being the institution of the "Onward" Juvenile Temple, which has been formed in conifliction with the . "Hope of Appleton "lodge of Good Tempters. Brother B Preston, D.S J.T., performed the ceremony. About 150 members of the Sunbeam " and " Lilly " Juvenile Temples, under the care of their respective superintendents, Sister Birkhall and Brother C Webb, were present, tegether with a number of members and friends of the order. There I were 31 juveniles and 12 adults initiated members of the new temple. The following officers were installed for the I quarter :—C.T., Brother R Parsons ; VT., Sister J W I Thompson,; P.C.T., Brother R ; R. 9., Brother D T Rathbone„• KS., Brother W Hill; Treas., Brother Isaac , Taylor ; Chap., Sister 51 A Hill ; Marshal, Brother H Taylor ; Guard. Brother W H Phytbian ; Sti., Brother Thomas Hollins ' • AS , Brother J E Jones; D.M , Sister , M Harrison. Addresses were delivered by Brothers Preston, Webb, and Turton, and Sister Birkhall. The temple, which is in charge of Brother J Thompson (superintendent) and Sister Mrs Thompson (assistant superintendent), promises to be very successful. SHOCKING DEATH NEAR FRODSHAM.—On Tuesday even- ing a boy, named Wm. Chantler, aged 15, met with his death at the Rancorn Boneworks, Sutton, near Frodsham, under very shocking circumstances. It appeared that Chant- ler asked a man named Wm. Lowe with whom he worked, whether he could go and grease the straps in the char- rooms. Lowe directed the boy to attend to the straps in the lower rooms, but not to enter the upper portion of the premises. Nothing more was seen of the boy, and it was presumed when he had completed his task he had gone home with the rest of the men. At eight o'clock in the evening, as he had not returned home, his father, who is coachman and gardener to the Rev Edward Marsden, of Sutton, became anxious and went to the works. He in- quired of a man named Joseph Hind—a night retort man— whether his son had been seen about. He replied that he was not then about, but the two men instituted a search in the works. On going to the upper char-room a horrible sight met their gaze, the body of Chantler being found ter- ribly mutilated amongst the machinery. Nearly every bone in the lifeless body was broken, while the upper portion of the skull was completely shattered, the brains being scat- tered over the adjacent wall. The two men were unable to summon courage to extricate the body, and sent for P.C. Egerton, who removed it from the machinery. It is con- jectured that the boy, acting against his instructions, at- tempted to remove the strap from one pulley to snottier while the machinery was in motion, and that he was caught . by the flying wheel and killed almost instantly.—An in- , quest relative to the occurrence was held before Mr , way, coroner, at Sutton, yesterday morning, when a verdict ' of "Found dead "was returned. THE newly-formed Liberal Council for the Newton Parliamentary Division has got to work. The first meeting was held at Earlestown on Tuesday evening, when there was a large attendance of representatives from the various districts. The president, vice-presidents, and other officers were ap- pointed, after which the Chairman! Mr. CHARLES PILKINGTON, J.P., intimated tha4 Colonel MCCORQUODALE had been seen in- formally as to allowing his name to be brought forward with a view to his becoming the Liberal candidate for the Division. Colonel MCCORQUODALE had expressed the wish to be in a position to help someone else rather than accept the position himself; but practically left the matter in the hands of the Liberal party. As it was not for that meeting to come to a decision, the question of a can- didate was left over to a future meeting, though it was pretty evident that the feeling of the Council was highly favourable to the nomination of the Colonel. The Council afterwards proceeded to pass a resolution in support of the Government, which was backed up by effective and pertinent speeches. The new organisation has made a good start, and we trust it will have a long and successful career.

THE Conservatives of Warrington won the election in South-West Ward on Monday, but the victory is not one of which they can feel very proud. Not that we would suggest that they will not have a good representative in Councillor JOLLEY ; he has promised his , party to give a party vote when required, though at the same time, with curious in- consistency, he professes to deprecate intro- ducing politics into municipal matters. The Liberals have been beaten, but they have the: consolation of knowing that they come out of the contest with clean hands. So far as they are concerned, the new Cor- rupt Practices Act has been respected to the letter. Some of the lesser lights of the Conservative party have, however, we have good good reason for saying, infringed the Act; treating has been resorted to in the old bold bad fashion, and for the moment it has succeeded. Possibly those who are now congratulating themselves upon their "sharp practice" may see the matter in a different light when evidence is brought against them in the Police Court. It is not 'pleasant to engage in such a task, 1 but the law ought to be vindicated so as to make it what it is designed to be— a terror to evil doers. Mr. C. S. BURGESS, the Liberal candidate, made a good fight ; he has won his spurs, if he has not won the election ; and has paved the way for success in the future. A good deal has been said about the Tory majority being so large as 16. The Conservatives have short memories, ind are therefore oblivious of the f&ct that Alder- man CKOSFIELD won the election for the Liberals by exactly the same majority in 1880. The Liberals have lost a seat amongst the Councillors, but, having gained one by the election of Mr. CROSFIELD as Alderman, both parties may for the present cry each other " quits."

ST PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.

By the Irish inhabitants of Widnes, forming so large a pro- portion of the population, St Patrick's Day is usu tlly hon- oured with demonstrations of various kinds. Unfortunately on Tuetday, the weather was very unpropitious for any out- door di•play, rain falling heavily the greater portion of the afternoon. By many people the day was observed as a holiday, and they were to be seen walking the streets adorned with the "shamrock" of the Emerald Isle, or a green favour. Flags were displayed In several localities, and there were sounds of merriment from many domiciles. 'the members of St Mary's League of the Cross had inten- ded to have a demonstration, and a procession numbering about 1,000 persons started from the schools, but after walk- ing over part of the route decided upon, was compelled to return, owing to the stermy weather. The tit Mary's Yonag Men's Society Brass Band was in attendance. Toe procession was followed by a number of boisterous youths, who when passing Sims Cross Board School, commenced to throw stones, several of the missiles crashing through the windows of that building. There was, however, nothing approaching a disturbance. In the evening an entertain- ment, under the auspices of St Mary's Catholic school, was held in the Volunteer Hall. The room was crowded. An excellent programme was gone through, the following tak- ing part :—Madame Lalor, of Liverpool, Miss A Flint, of Liverpool, Messrs Farrell and Wilmot, of Glasgow, and Paddy Watson, of Manchester. A choir of boys from St Mary's school, conducted by Mr Faulkner, sang several part songs, and St Mary's Brass Band played several selections of music in good style. The second part was occupied with an Irish sketch, the characters being ably represented by Miss E Riley, Miss N McMahon, Messrs .7 Carroll, J McMa- hon, J Gordon, T Stoner, and James Quinn At the new schoolroom connected with St Bede's Chapel, Appleton, the 6th annual concert was given, and there was a good midi. ence. Songs and ballads were given by the choir and the members of the congregation, and a very pleasant evening was spent. The Rev Father Finegan delivered an appro- priate address.

CONTRAVENTION op isn.CANAL BOATS ACT—At Run- corn Petty Seseions, on Monday, Messrs Fellows and Mot, ton, carriers, Wolverhampton, were charged with not having the canal boat Madras registered as a dwelling-house in con- formity with the Canal Boate Acts, 1877 and 1884.—Mr J Farrington, canal boat inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, proved finding the boat on the canal between Aston and Norton. The boat was not "lettered, marked, and numbered" on both sides, as required by the Acts.—Mr Joseph Bridgewater appeared for the defendants. I who, he said, owned 200 boats. He read a letter tram the firm in which they stated that their dock was situate some distance from the main line of the canal, and they had given instructions four months before the close of the year for the boat to be lettered on both sides, but they supposed It had not been in the dock in the interim. They admitted there had been a technical violation of the law, but thought the case would be met by the withdrawal of the summons. —Mr Farrington said on the earns day he might have sum-1 moned the defendants in respect to a dozen other boats.—A fine of 51 and costs, lle Bd, was imposed. Clarkson said about five o'clock on the previous afternoon a procession of the members of the League of the Cross connected with the Lugsdale Catholic Chapel, of which the Rev Father Clarke is priest, took place. As the proceesion was passing the end of Waterloo-road he saw the prisoner with a nusnber of ether young men, armed with sticks, set upon a man unknown, and caused a terrible noise in the street.—The prisoner was then charged with assaulting Emma Gilooley, a reepectably-dreased young woman, wife of a labourer living at 44, Major Cross-street.—The prosecu- tor said on the previous afternoon she was standing at the corner of Major Cross-street. She was wear'ng a dark red neckerchief, and the prisoner came up to her and asked '4 Where is your green." t- omeone called out "Take the -- handkerchief off her," and the prisoner struck her across the breast with a stick. ' ArrAcznia WITH A POKER AT WIDNES.—At Widues Police Court, on Monday, Reter Ryley, a labourer, was , charged with unlawfully wounding Mary Treacy, wife of John Treacv, labourer, Pear-street, Widnes. The prosecu- trix deposed that about nine o'clock on Saturday night last the prisoner's brother came to her house and ceased a dis- turbance. With assistance she put him outside, and looked the door. In a few minutes afterwards he returned with the prisoner. A woman named Mrs Roach, whe Was in the house, wanted to go* home, and when going through the ' doorway someone struck her. Witness went to see who it was, and she received a blow in the eve by the prisoner's brother. Then the prisoner came across the road and struck I her with the poker produced across the head and other parts of the body. Her apron was also covered with blood. Bhe felt much pain, and never slept all night in consequence.l She gave the prisoner no provocation, and never spoke tels him at all.—By the prisoner; She never threw a kettle of water over hien nor had she a hammer in her hand.—The husband of the last witness said he saw the prisoner strike his wife with the poker. His wife gave the prisoner no pro. vocation.—Bridget Walsh, 27, Pear-street, corroborated.— By the prisoner: She saw Mrs Treacy throw a kettle of boiling water at the prisoner, but she did not see it go on him. Mrs Treacy had a hammer in her hands.—Dr Mac- Donnell said on Saturday sight, about ten o'clock, the prosecutrix came to his house. She was suffering from a scalp wound. On removing the hair he found a lacerated wound fully an inch long and penetrating to the bone. There were also contusions on the left side of the face, and the left side of the hand. She had lost a great quantity of blood, for her clothes were covered with it. The prosecutrix also appeared very weak. The poker produced would be a likely weapon to produce such a wound, and considerable violence would have to have been used to inflict it. The prosecutrix was not well now, and suffered a great deal of pain.—P.C. Thompson deposed to apprehending the prisoner. who, when charged, said he used no weapons, and alleged that prosecutrix threw a kettle of water over him.—The pri- soner was committed for trial. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday. Present : Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton (in the chair), the Rev J Lock- wood/ Messrs W Handley, T Norman, Hightisid, Stokes, Whittaker, Aaron, Speakman, Pickering, Krowles, Mclntyre, Jackson, Weir, Rigby, Derbyshire, Wallington, Acton, Smith, Lewis, It Aahton, and H Linaker (clerk). THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.—The Assessment Com- mittee recommended that the alert's salary for the past year be £B5. Tee year previous it was £195. The committee further recommended that Mr W Handley should accom- pany the clerk to Chester in respect to the appeal against the county rate basis. The recommendations were adoptel It was explained that the clerk was paid according to the work he did for the committee. FINAECE.—Mr W Handley said the county precept for the next half year, payable on the 23rd met, was an in- crease of £2643 upon the corresponding half year, and it had been necessary to revise the estimates presented at the last meeting and increase the rate by a farthing in the £, making it 7id in the £ —The report was adopted. SUNDAY CLOSING.—A petition in favour of closing public.. houses on Sunday was placed on the table.—Mr Mclntyre moved that the petition be signed by the chairman on be- half of the Board and forwarded to the members of Parlia- ment for the division for presentation in the House of Com- mons. He was not a teetotaller and he did not advocate this resolution on behalf of teetotallers, but it must be pa- tent to anyone that both in town and country the effect of the sale of intoxicating liquor On Sunday was worse than on any of the other six. There was more drunkenness on the Sunday than on any other day in the week, and as butchers' and bakers' shops were lint on that day he thought the public-houses should also be shut.—Mr Aaron Seconded the motioa with very great pleasure. In Weston on Sunday there were men to be seen reeling about the streets in a filthy and drunken condition, and there was more drunkenness on the Sabbath than on any other day In the week. He also thought the closing of public-houses would be a boon to the publicans.—The motion was carried. . . . .

RESIGNATION OF MR WRIORT.—The Chairman read the following letter from Mr P Wright, relieving officer for the Runcorn district.—" I regret to inform you that during the past week I have been unable through sickness to attend to my duties, and as I am still very weak, perhaps it would be better if I considered the question of resigning, and I should therefore feel obligwl if you would please submit this letter as my resignation to the Guardians, at their next meeting, and I hope the Guardians will favourably consider the ap- plication which I now make for a superannuation allowance after my 30 years servicew"—Mr Norman said that the long

and faithful murices of Mr Wright deserved the earnest at- tention and consideration of the Board, and he moved that a committee consisting of the Revs J W N Tanner, J Lockwood, and Messrs William Handley, T Norman, Henry Meld, John Ashton, John Weir, Edward Aaron, Charles Rigby, and Mclntyre, should consider the amount of super- annuation allowance that should be granted.—The Clerk pointed out that the Board could not exceed two-thirdt of the salary—Mr Norman remarked that Mr. Wrii.ht had served the Board well for 30 years, and he thought his ap- plication deserved their favourable consideration.—Mr Aaron thought it a waste of time to appoint a committee. (Bear, hear.) Mr Wright must have been a good servant to retain his position so long, and he begged to give notice that at the next meeting he would mere that Mr Wright should be given a superannuation allowanse of two-thirds of Mesalary. They would thus show their respect for a faithful servant, and encourage the officers of the Board.— Mr Jackeon seconded the motion.—Mr Darbyshire said he had known Mr Wright since his (the speaker's) infancy, and they must all know that he had done his duty well, or he would not have been their servant up to the present time. He should be glad, if he did not happen to be present at the next meeting, to now declare his approval of giving Mr Wright all the law would allow them. (Hear, bear, and applause.)—Mr Handley then moved that Mr Wright's resignation be accepted. He did not think, taking Mr Wright as a whole, that they would ever get a better ser- vant—Mr Lockwood seconded the propositien with a few sympathetic remarks, and it was carried unanimously.—Mr Norman moved, and Mr Aaron seconded, that a successor be advartisal for at a salary of £lOO a year.—Mr. Rigby moved, and Mr Weir seconded, an amendment that the salary be £Bo.—The original motion war carried by six votes to five—The committee nominated by Mr Norman was then appointed, and they were also authorised to receive the applications for the vacant post. Thera was no other public business.

THE STRETTON SEWERAGE SCHEME.—The Rev. Canon Dodd and Mr. Joseph Brocklehurst appeared before. the Authority, as a deputation from the ratepayers, with refer- ence to the proposed scheme for the draining of a certain portion of Stretton.—The Rev. Canon Dodd said the rate- payers contended that the scheme proposed by the Authority was altogether unnecessary, and even if it were necessary the cost was three or four times what it should be by ordin- ivy tenders. The ratepayers had obtained tenders for draining the overflow from the common pond, which caused the pollu- tion first complained of, the highest of which was about £l5. Whereas the Authority proposed to spend £l5O. The Sur- veyor to the Authority had expressed himself to the effect that the ratepayers' scheme was sufficient.—The Chairman said the Authority was always averse to putting a township to unnecessary expense. If the township had abated the nuisance the matter would never have corne before the Authority at all. The Authority could not sanction the scheme propounded by the deputation, but if the nuisance was abated nothing more would be beard of the matter. Mr Brocklehurst said Mr Marston was quite satisfied with the new scheme.—Canon Dodd said when they had spent their money the Authority might say the nuisance was not abated.—The Chairman : So we should It there WU no abatement.—The Clerk pointed out that Mr Marston was the original complainant, and if he was satisfied the rate- payers would bear nothing from the Board.—The deputation then withdrew.

EPIDEMIQ OF MEASLES: TERRIBLE SPREAD OF ?RR INFECTION.—The Medical Officer presented the following report :—" In my last special report I mentioned that infor- mation bad reached me of an outbreak of measles at Preston Brook and Preston-o'th'-hill I am now able to give you particulars. On March 4th and March 10th I visited these localities and discovered that measles existed in no less than 18 houses, in which I found 30 children suffering or .conva- lescent from measles. I will not burden you with details of names of occupiers of premises and names and ages of patients of all of which I have, however, a careful record,. The disease has been propogated mainly by school infec- tion, the schools have been cloeed and I recommend they, be limews.sbed and disinfected previous to being re-opened. I have further to report that on March 12th, information reached me of an outbreak of measles In Kingsley. On the 13th I visited this township and found that the disease was present in 40 houses (2 of these are In Kingewood Forest), and that 71 children were suffering or convalescent from measles. Two original foci of infection were found at op- posite ends of the village. In both of these cases the in- faction was imported from Runcorn three weeks previously Is my inspection, and from these foci the disease has spread like wildfire through the village, by the highly popular and eminently successful method of school infection ; a method which was vigorously maintained for three weeks, with school attendance daily dwindling down, till on the day of his visit one solitary urchin turned up for the day in the Infant school, when I fortunately intervened to save him from the trouble of further attendance by closing what had been a perfect hotbed of infection. I am happy to be able to state that a death roll has only jot comrnemced, one case, a child of Mr Lightfoot having succumbed. Surely some- thing should have been done before this. Cannot school- masters be firmly requested (especially in Board schools) to communicate at once with me In each cases P 1 venture ta suggest that the Sanitary Authority semi a circular note to all schoolmasters under the control of public bodies, and private schoolmasters for that matter, requesting them to inform me at once of the occurrence of the popular school zymotic, measles, and scarlet fever. Again I have received in formation from private medical source that in Halton there are 22 cases in 11 different houses, reaching to Stockham. The schools should also be closed here. Since I entered the Board-room I have been informed there are 55 cases in Halton parish including Stockham. At my visit I urged all the usual preventative measures. The Medical Officer also reported a death from typhoid fever at Weston Point. The outbreak was evidently caused by " filth "; there is overcrowding and much poverty; morals bad. The premises had been disinfected, and the bedding burned. Compansation should be made." The Medical Officer remarked that there was a total of 166 cases of measles in the union.—The Rev J Lockwood said to show how suddenly thi epidemic had come upon them, he might state that on Saturday moraing there was not a single case in Halton. Dr Carruthers would bear him out if he were present. In the afternoon there were 11 cases, on Sunday morning there I were 42, and that morning there were 55 cases. He had seen the whole 55 before he came to the Board.—The Medical Officer said he should recommend the immediate closing of schools where a single case appeared. When measles broke out in this fashion, it swept through the dis- trict Ilk a wave. The Authority had no compulsory power to close schools, but they could make a strong recommenda- tion. He bad seven patients in one house. There had only been one death from the disease—Mr Lewis asked if the outbreak could be accounted for.—The Medical Officer re- plied by personal infection Runcorn was • favourite place for getting those things from. You can get anything you like from Runcorn. (Laughter.> The disease seems to be of an unusually infections type.—The Rev .1 Lockwood: It seems to be very mild.—The Medical officer said out of 71 patients in Kingsley only one had died, that was about per cent, whereas the the average deaths from measles in England and Wales was from S to 5 per cent. Mr Darbyshire remarked that it was rumoured that at one public school the infection had spread from the child of a teacher.—The Medical Officer said he had ascertained that two other cases broke out on the same day. He added that he was anticipating that every township in the Union would be visited by the die- ease.—On the motion of the Rev J Lockwood, seconded by Mr Wallington. it was decided that the .nedical officer's sug- gestion should be carried out. SEwsca Drrat OFT ii&LTOII•LANE, Ilsurow.—The In- spector reported that he had served notice in reference to this matter as directed, but nothing as yet bad been done respecting it. He hal received a communication from the agent to Sir Richard Brooke, to which he had replied. He I had also Been the agent of the other property, who stated I that so far as their property was concerned the nuisance would be immediately abated.—The Clerk stated that from information he had received he thought something would shortly be done to improve the present condition of the ditch.—Alter some consideration it was ultimately agreed to adjourn the matter for a fortnight. TYPHOID Fsvan Cams.—The Inspector also 'sported that there had been a fatal case of typhoid fever at Lunt 8- row, Weston. He had disinfec.tad the room, and he had deemed it advisable to burn the bed, and he now asked that compensation be given for the same.—lt was decided that another bed be supplied at suggested by the inspector, and that the cost of removing and deetroying the infected ma-
betel be paid.—. The Inspector presentsd an account incur- red in the removal of two fever patients from Kingsley in Moveraber last, and it was decided that the Same be paid.

- WATIR ANALYS/S.—Certificates of analysis of water from a pump and well to cottage premises at Stratton, and from a pump and well at farm premises at Newton-by-Daresbury were read, and both were left in the hands of the inspector to deal with.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. Mr Charles Littler, slater, , Greenway-road, Runcorn, met with a serious accident on Thursday. For the purpose of repairing the roof of Camden Wesleyan school he bad fired two ladders, one resting upon the ground and the other, blocked by a piece of wood, reached from the trough to the ridge of the roof. Whilst he was upon this aesond ladder it slipped, and be was rlalling down the sloping roof when he dashed hi hammer into the glitter'. Bathos main- tained himself for some momenta. but before aid could arrive the slate smashed, he slipped to the edge of the roof, and then fell to the ground, a distance of about I 2 feet. Re alighted heavily upon his back, and was picked up uncon- scious, and conveyed home. Dr Robinson was quickly in attendance, but the condition of the injured man was tech that he deemed it wise to defer an examination.. Later on he pronounced that no bones were broken, but that the, muscles of the spine were seriously Injured. The acci- dent is the more unfortunate as Mr Littler contemplated paying a visit to Canada early in the spring.

TRH HOME IRON TRADE. The English iron market continues quiet. The Glasgow warrant market has been steady this week, and the fluctuations have been trifling. It cannot be said, however, that there are signs of improve- ment in the etate of trade or any prospect of a better de- mand for pig-iron setting in from abroad. At present the demand is falling off owing to Scotch iron being relatively higher than any other class of iron. Makers find a diffi- culty in making sales, although willing to take less than current rates. On Wednesday, closing buyers of warrants offered 41s 4id cash, and 41e Eld a month, sellers asking !2,1 per ton more. In the North of England, the pig-iron trade has kept the same quiet tone during the Vast week. But as the shipping season is approaching, It is believed that a decided improvement will take place in foreign ship- men ts. —lron. MEDlculics, ELISTIO BT3CHINGS, CERMICLLS. LYMM LIBERAL ASSOCIATION-. A public meeting was held under the auspices of Hsi, Association on Monday evening, in the Minion Hall, Lymm, to hear addresses on " Liberalism and Conserva- tism : A review and a lesson." Mr. E. Brewtnall presided, and amongst those present were Messrs Milne, Swenwick, and Welford. The Chairman, in his introductory remarkerreferred to the condition of the working classes fifty or sixty yeareago, when the Radical movement commenced in earnest. One of the earliest efforts, he said, that was made to change the existing state of things was that which afterwards became known as the celebrated Blanket March. The "Bianketeers," as they were called, assembled on the site of the present Free Trade Hall, Manchester, to consider their grievances. (A Voice : There were some in Lymm.) The movement, be thought, began in Staffordshire, where the colliers-were in such a wretched condition that they determined to draw two loads of coal to London and to lay their case before the Prince Regent. The Manchester working-men determined, if possible, to improve upon that idea, and to make a pil- grimage to London to lay their case before the authorities. To perform the journey each one Was provided with a blanket, as they intended to sleep anywhere on the way and carry their food with them. At this the authorities took alarm and said these men were revolutionists. There- fore, by force they dispersed the " blanketeers." La 1819 took place the celebrated Peterloo maeracre. The working- men met together in great numbers to consider their condi- tion, bat the meeting, although it was a peaceable one, was charged by troops, eleven being killed and about 600 wounded. (A Voice: Dark ages.) What was the condition of the working people now compared to then ? Food was cheap and good, working-men generally were in an Average state of comfort, and the pauper roll was less now than it had been for a great many years. How cheap now was clothing, and how great the revolution that had taken place In education. From a humble beginning the work had gone on until there was something like 6,000,000 children now attending excellent schools. Education for the people was now so well organised that the wonderful effects that were being produced were patent to all. He °meat that the result would be the political and social elevation of England, for It was well known that we were In our technical knowledge far behind other coun- tries, and in everything that would lead to the supremacy of England in the manufacturing world. Although much had been done for the improvement of workmen's dwellings they were not yet satisfied with the result. All would know that a Royal Commission, with the Prince of Wales at its head, was about to make a report upon the dwellings of the poor, and he hoped that some great scheme would be forth- coming for the universal improvement of workmen't dwell- ings, in order that men might live in more comfort and happiness. Politically, now, the working-man was the ruler of the country, and not a cypher. Democracy was now in the seat of power, and with the working-men of Eng- land rested the future destinies of the country. Demos WRS the king, and he had no doubt as to the result. The reforms that had been accomplished were due to the actions of the Liberal party, which worked entirely for the benefit of the masses. (Applause.) Mr W Milne then delivered an address. Referring to the work to be done to return Liberal candidates at the next election for the division of Mid-Cheshire, he said that he re- membered one election when Lymm polled ten to one against the Liberals. At the coming election they must reverse that state of things. (Applause.) It was not only not impos- sible, but it was most likely, that they should have &liberal majority in that part of the district. They stood uncom- monly well to accomplish It if they would only put their shoulders to the wheel. They knew who had opposed the Franchise Bill; the same party that had opposed every bene- fit that had been attempted to be cenferred upon the people of Eegland. The thine that were intended for the benefit of the whole people were those which the Tories pure and simple were bound to oppose by the very nature and condi- tion of their minds. (Applause.) He concluded by referring to the peace question, and said that to him it seemed a ter- rible thing that, with the profession we made of Christianity, it should be found possible to go to war. Mr Watford spoke on the land question. Ire wished then to seriously consider what was known under the title of the unearned increment of land. If they looked at that question from a land-owner's point of view, probably they would find that they should act precisely as did the land-owners. There- fore, be was not quarreling with land-owners, but he said that the law of the land put them into a position which they should not be permitted to occupy. He would give an illustration, although the case might be rather an aggravated one. Supposing a person owned land which had for many years been unproductive, and some person stumbled across some article in that land that Was. of public value, such as coal, lead, or- iron. Immediately men of capital and of speculative turn erected works in the neighbourhood, aid the hitherto unproductive land became immediately of great value. The one who owned the lan& had not made the value, but the men who had invested their capital had dbne so by the erection of works and the refresh- ing of trade and industry in the neighbourhood. But yet the one who reaped the most benefit was the owner, who perhaps had never spent a penny on the land which in fature would yield him a good income. Out of that land rose the great value which politicians were calling the have that increased value—that-thos who e unearned increment. Some said not the landowner, but the made the value of the land should have the benefit; and' they State, m they were the people at large. ili3 feeling was that it should not all go to the benefit of the owner. (Applause ) Proceeding, he said that the object of the series of meetings they had been holding in Lymm recently was to educate those amongst them who for the first time were admitted into the pale of the constitution. Those-present would. shortly for the first time find their nameraon an electoral register. (Hear, hear.) In fact, they were now passirig. through a revolution, quiet and bloodless, but none the less. one, accomplishing more in its ultimate consequences than the bloody revolution of France nearly a century ago. At the next general election they would have an opportunity of expressing at the poll their views in regard to national affairs, and he thought the working men had as. earnest, and as abiding an interest in the well-being of the country as had those who plumed themselves upon being superior in intelligence and in social position. The work-. ing man might Boon lose his all, but the pees- might always save a little out of .his.much. When it wara said that the admission of the woraing-ci assea to the fra,,,, chine was a danger to the fabric of the constitution, and wan exposing it to the whims and fancies of uneducated men, they, the Liberals, cast the charge back upon they who, telligence enough to enable them to decide what wars and made it, and said that there was amongst working men, in, what was not good for themselves. (Applause.) Them had never before existed such &reason as did now why working- men should consider political sebjects, and it leas with the object of exciting a desire to understand-well the rjulitical questions of the future that the Liberal Committee‘af Lynam had organised their series of meetings, Which were intended to be largely educational in their character. Having re- viewed past political reform, Mr. Welford asked which party ago 11 It was the Liberal was it that had fired politics mat of the SlaVial end narrow :areas that the PeCrole of to-day rut_ party. aw.hdictah itthtehey yweorweefidfttyhey were in= improved condition. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Wiiii tin Gainer was summoned for ill-treating a horse on the 11th inst, and John Connor for causing it to be worked. The horse was one of a pair dragging a 'bus, and was seen at Latchford by P.C. 10, who noticed that it was very lame. Evidence was also given that the horse was entirely unfit for road work.—Gainer was discharged and Connor was fined 203 and costs.

ILLEGAL PURCHASE OF LEAD —James Warburton, said to belong to Northwich, was charged with having on the 23th February, he being a dealer in old metals, purchased contrary to the statute, leis than 112 lbs of old metal. Ser- geant Harrington spoke to having seen the defendant go into Mr Cheetham's house, at Lymm, on the day named, and afterwards come out with the lead produced which only weighed 38Ibs. • The defendant took in with him some rub- bing stones which he did not bring out with him, and when apprehended he said he had not bought the lead, but given rubbing stones in exchange.—Mrs Cheatham was called, and said that she gave the defendant the lead and did not take any rubbing stones in exchange.—A. fine of 10s and costs was imposed, APPLICATION.—AS application was made on behalf of Mrs Sumner, of the Plough Hotel, Lymm, for an extension of hours on the 10th April, on the occasion of the lawn tennis ball.—Mr John Lee, of the Fleece Hotel, made a sim- ilar application for the 30th March, the occasion being a ball.—Extensiona till two o'clock were granted in each case. UNLICENSED Dons.—Dan Boyd, of Lymm, was charged With having kept two dogs without licenses, and was fined 10s 2nd costs in each case.—Henry Collins, also of Lymm, was charged with having kept an unlicensed dog, but the case was dismissed. FOOTBALL.

Secretariea of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning,

EARLESTOWN (25D TEAM) V. EARLES TOWN RAMBLERS (15T.)—These teams met on the ground of the first-named on Saturday, in the presence of a fairly good number of spectators. The home team won by six goals to one. VULCAN v. DitovuDEN,—These teams met on Saturday on the ground of the latter, and a pleasant but one- sided game resulted in a win for Vulcan by one goal (by Gorch), one try, and nine minor points to one try. Massey and Varley scored the tries for Vulcan. WARRINGTON EXCELSIOR V. ST. BARNABAS (FIRST TuAzt). —The above clubs met for the third time this season on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and a very pleasant and well-contested game resulted in a well-deserved victory for the Excelsiors by two goals, two tries, one disputed try, and four minor points to nil. HAYDOCE ST. JAMES'S V. GOLBORNE.—This match was played at Golborne on Saturday, and after a nice game resulted in a draw of one goal each. The second teams of the above met at Haydock, and after a very one-sided game resulted in a win for ihe home team by five goals to one. It may be remarked, as this is the last match this season for the St. James's second team, that they have never once been beaten all through the season. RUNCORN " OLD Boys" V. WIDNES VICTORIA.—Tb is match, which was played on the ground of the former club on Saturday afternoon, proved of a very interesting nature, owing. probably, to the equality of the teams and the fact of lb being well contested. The game resulted in a well- earned victory for the home team, their score being one try (obtained by Johnson) and four minor points, and tlAt of the visitors two minor points. The following constituted the respective teams :—Old Boys : Full-back, W Wishlade ; three-quarter backs, W Knight, F H Harvey, and W Tickle; half-backs, B Williamson and J Steele; forwards, J Shaw, W E C Harvey, W Shaw, Higgins, T Night, E Howard, W Catterall, J Leyland, and J Johnson. Victoria: Fall-back, R Charles ; three-quarter backs, R Lea, W Bar- ber, and W Peters; half-backs, T Gleave and W Phytham ; forwards, J Barber. T Davies, Walsh, Sadler, Cooper, P Hunt, W Lomax, S Thomas, and J Ray. RUNCORN V. WAVERTREE (2nd Tnems.)—The return fix- ture h,t,veen these teams was played at Runcorn on Satur- day before a large number of spectators, and a pleasant but a very one-sided game resulted in the home team scoring four goals, five tries and eleven minor points to Wavertree nil. The home team never played a better game, their smart play and running being frequently applauded. For Wayertree Nichols, Dodd, Fraser, and Jones played a hard game. The tries were obtained by Lunt (3), Clarke (3), Antrobus, Janion, and Orme, Sanwball kicking the goals. Teams: Runcorn: Stubbs, back; Lunt, Riley, and Andres. three-quarter backs; Antrobus and Whitby, half- backs •, Clarke (captain), Janina, Cox, Orme, aittins, Dun- bavand, Abrams, Snowball, and Raffe, forwards. Waver- tree : Morton, back; Dodd, Pownall, and Cawley, three- quarter backs; Nicols (captain) and Gerrard, half-backs; Parker, Foster, Jones, Dugdale, Fraser, Thomas, Leadbetter, Raisbeck, and Cameron, forwards. . .

WARRINGTON (ASSOCIATION) V. WHISTON.—A return match was played between these clubs on Saturday on the ground of the former off Kuntsford-road, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by two goals to none. The after- noon being very favourable, an early start was made, and for some time the Whiston team had to act strictly on the defensive. The ball was kept in close proximity to the visitors' goal,and more than once the Warrington men very nearly scored. After about ten minutes or a quarter of an hours play, however, the Whistonians began to take the iad quickly scored the first goal. Before ends werejobanged they Put BoVler fie4l tgl their Credit. Subs setinently the Cofit.::twaa viageo very evenly between the two teams, the only noticeable feature of it being the some- what irregular play of the Warrington men. The Warring- ton team was as follows :—Goal, Woodward; backs, Davies (captain) and Royston; half backs, Walton, Pearson, and Jones; centre, Matthews; left wing, E Parker and J Gray; right wing, Siddie and Webster. FISHWICK RAMBLERS v. EARLESTOWN.—The Earlestown team journeyed to Preston on Saturday, and met the Fish- wick Ramblers at Walton Brow, before 800 spectators. Dempsey kicked off for the home team, and Harrison, the visitors' goalkeeper, had soon to fist out a good shot by Greenwood. Toe Ramblers gained a corner, Saul putting the ball right under the bar, but the goalkeeper just saved at the expense of another corner, which came to nothing. The visitors now had a look in and gained a corner, Sims even- , tually playing the ball over the line. The game was now very even, but Earlestown playing well togetsher scored their fret goal from the foot of Ellison. This put new life into the game. Half-time was called, with the score stand- leg—Earlestown one, Ramblers none. After change of ends the Ramblers had a scrimmage in front of Earlestown goal, and Gerard scored the first goal for his side, Dempsey tak- ing care of the goalkeeper. Earlestown bad a corner at the other end, but the ball was got away, and Baverstock, who put in a grand long shot, scored goal No. 2. The Ramblers played with more combination, and scored three other goals —Greenwood two and Saul one—thus winning by five goals to one.

WARRINGTON v. ALTRINCIUM.—In the presence of about 1,500 spectators, the return match between these clubs was played on the Warrington ground on Saturday, when the visitors suffered defeat. The turf was dry and in good con- dition, and was fav urable to fast•play. A capital game was witnessed, some of the play being very smart, and when no aide was called the score stood :—Warrington, one goal, one goal from disputed try, four tries, and eight minor pints, to Altrincham nil. Individual play was best shown by Barnes, who throughout the match fully atoned for his inferior display against Broughton. Massey, as usual, was very useful, his speed and kicking into touch being invalu- able. Warren was in a good humour, and exhibited a little of his old form. His partner, Gilbert, also did a vast amount of work, and was unselfish ; of the forwards the most prominent were—Fairfield, Turner, Dillon, Jolly, Rigby, and Haves. Altrincham were best represented by Smith, Brown, Kenyon, and Myles. Teams :—Warrington: T Walsh, back ; J T Massey, T Barnes, and W Speakman, three-quarter backs •, J E Warren and E Gilbert, half backs • H Ashton (captain). Fairfield, Turner, J Rigby, W Dillon, J R Calvert, W Povey, W Hayes, James Jolley, and F R Turner, forwards. Altrincham : T Bab- ington, back; J Warburton, T Cowell), and J Brown, three- quarter backs; R B Smith (haptain) and J Lear, half backs; J Myles, R Moreton, Li Kenyon, W Faulkner A Blease, A Bamford, T Farrell, W Whitehead, F H Long, forwards. WAVERTREE v. RoNconN.—The return match between " these clubs was played on Saturday, a goodly number of spectators being present. A pleasant and well.contested game was witnessed, although the result—three goals, a try, and two minor points for Runcorn, against a try and one minor point—may seem to indicate that it was rather one- sided. Wavertree won the toss, and on Wright starting the leather Foster failed to return, missing his kick. This enabled Woods to get in, and he followed it up by scoring a try for Runcorn within a few minutes from the start, which he improved upon by registering the major poist. After a tight scrimmage in the centre, H Hughes made a capital run, eluding Foster, and registered a second try for the visitors, Woods was again entrusted with the place, and he easily accomplished the task. A long pass subsequently gave Wright an opportunity, and he dropped an excellent goal from the field of play. Runcorn still continued the pressure, and before half-time compelled Foster to touch down, Wavertre., in the meantime, having only one minor point to their credit. With such a balance in their favour, the Runcorn lads took *natters easier in the second half, contenting themselves with defensive play; while the villagers made desperate efforts to improve their position. From the scrimmage which followed, Beszant got hi oppor- tunity, and a short dodging run ended in a meritorious try. On Schweitzer being called upon to take the place he made a bad job of it. The visitors after this made a determined assault on the home quarters, and Foster was called upon to stop some capital runs, but after Speakman had made an attempt to drop a goal Foster was compelled to touch down. Until no-side was called tta leather was scarcely allowed to come out of Wavertree 25, and the game ended as above in- dicated. Wavertree F Foster, back; Schweitzer, T Woodward, and Singleton, three•quarter backs; W Peters and J Grierson, half backs; T Edwards, W L Goodman, W Parry, G Newman, G Grierson, R Wilcock, W H Sutton, E &saint, and C Wakefield, forwards. Runcorn W Hughes, back; H Speakman, T Johnson, and T Woods, three-quarter backs; Anderson and Hughes, half backs; Gatley, J Lewis, J Clark, J lleffland, W Mason, J Ford, It Roberts,W Wright, and W Cox. forwards.
WEST LANCASHIRE AND BORDER TOWNS RUGBY UNION.

LIVERPOOL CLUBS V. D;;;;I;" CLERS.—The first match of the above union under Rugby rules was played on Thursday at Runcorn. Considering that the day NM an off one, there was an excellent attendance, between four and five thousand spectators being present. The weather was all that could be desired, and everything tended to a suc- cessful inauguration of the association. There were several chanv.es in each team, the Liverpool contingent suffering most, Lycett, Al'sop, J B Lonsdale, Crosby, and J A Brodie being unable to play; nevertheless, substitutes of excellence were forthcoming, and when the teams stepped on the ground there was any amount of enthusiasm. The die- trict, who almost retained the advertised team, were well represented in the back division by Roberts Speakman, and W Hughes, who was very safe at full back, and the district captain was always ready and on the ball. In the forward franks Brayshay, Borthwick, and Holt were most prominent. The Liverpudlians were unfortunate in having a full back whom we may say at once appeared nervous, and he certainly failed badly at many critical points of the game. All the three-quarters played well, and both Butcher and Al'Farlane did a lot of work. Forward we have a good word for Wilcock, Bezant, and Holmes, the latter being especially prominent. The district lot, however, had the advantage almost throughout in the loose play, and the result of two goals, two tries, and four minor points to four minor points fully represents the general play.

The Queen drove in Hyde Park on Thursday morning, and in the afternoon returned to Windsor. Large numbers of people assembled in the park to see Her Majesty. Mr. Henry Lee, M.P., opening a bazaar on Wednesday at Buy, held that Congregationalism, regarded in its social, political, or religious aspects, was well suited to the present conditions of society. Sir Thomas Bazley, Bart., died suddenly on Wednesday at his residence, Riversleigh, Lytham, at the age of 88. The deceased baronet represented Manchester in Parliament for a period of 22 years, from 1858 to 1880.

The appeal of the Valtos crofters against the decision of Sheriff Substitute Black was argued before the Judges in Edinburgh on Thursday. The conviction was upheld, and the crofters will now have to undergo the sentence passed on them.

OF.ATH OF THE OLDEST INUABITANT IN WALES.—Sarah Ludwig, the oldest inhabitant in the Principality, has died at her cottage, Swansea, at the advanced age of 106 years. She was in receipt of parish relief for many years, and was in full possession of her faculties to the last.

SHOCKING Amin:Tr.—At Wyke, near Cleckheaton, on Wednesday evening, a wagon horse took fright at the " music " of a procession of the "Christian Army,' and plunged among the crowd. Many people were knocked down, and several were run over. A boy of 14 died on Thurs- day morning from his injuries, and about half a dozen other persons are lying seriously hurt. A BREWER HEAVILY FINED.—At Sedgley on Monday, John Kemberley, brewer, was fined £lOO and costs, and ordered to forfeit a number of vessels, for having defrauded the inland revenue by allowing his workmen to put some- thing in casks of beer in order to make it saleable as strong ale. It was stated that defendant had been previously fined £3OO for defrauding the inland revenue. THE RAILWAY RATES BILL.—The principal representa- tives of the leading railway companies which constitute the , Railway Association had a protracted meeting on Monday, and determined to press upon the Board of Trade the necessity of two statesmen of eminence being appointed members of the commission to which the Government pro- pose to refer the subject of the classification of the railway rates.

ROYAL Dnevrirro Room.—The Queen took a walk on Wednesday morning in the private grounds of Buckingham Palace. At three o'clock in the afternoon the Queen held a drawing room at Buckingham Palace, which, as it was the first her Majesty had held in person for a considerable period, was very largely attended, especially by debutantes, amone the latter being the Princess Louise of Wales. The weather was beautifully fine. The Qneen will hold a Privy Council at Windsor on or about the 27th mat; prior to her departure for Germany.

council of 300 members and an executive council of about 58 members. Each township was asked to choose their own representatives, and the members were elected according to the number of inhabitants. Nearly all the townships; certainly, all the most important townships had done that, and they had only to look around that room to see that those who had been chosen bad attended to the call. That was the first meeting of the Council, and it was to that Council that they must look for the return of a Liberal member for that division of the county. (Applause.) No doubt maey of the members had fought in battles in peat days, but he felt sure that in the Council would be young men whe at the next election would have the first opportunity of exercising the franchise; and they hoped that infusion of new blood in South-West Lancashire would enable them to reverse the regular run of Tory members which they had had for so many years. (Applause.) They were about tired of it, and he thought that division of South-West Lancashire was I about the most Liberal in its tendency. They had a hard I battle to fight, and they must work heartily together. They I might all have different individual opinions and ideas as to what sort of a candidate they should have. The Liberal party embraced almost every sart of idea, but he hoped they I would all have one idea above the others, and that one the returning of a Liberal to represent that division. They must sink their own private differences and join hand in hand and be determined to be successful. The first busi- ness of that new Council was the election of its officers, including an Executive Council, whose proceedings would have to be submitted for the approval of the General Council. They had expected Mr Powell, secretary of the Central Association, to be present to tell them something as to what their work would be. They did not yet know whether they would have to rely upon Liverpool as in the past, or whether that Association would have to do Its own work. The work of registration would be a very heavy I task, and they would also require to be "in touch" with the Parliamentary people of Liverpool and London. He ' concluded by intimating that it would be interesting to know 'how many of the out townships were represented at that I gathering, and he asked the representatives to hold up their bands. From the counting which ensued, it was gathered that Ashton-ia-Makerfield was represented by 27 persons, Bold 2, Golborne 23, Haydock 24, Newton, Earles- town, and Vulcan 44, and Rainhill 6; the chairman remark- ing that it would thus be seen that the principal townships were well represented. (Applauee.) The Chairman having stated that the first business was the appointment of a chairman for the new Liberal Associ- ation of the Newton Division of South West Lancashire, Mr Birkhead moved that Mr Charles Pilkington be elected to the post.—The Chairman said there were older and more influential names connected with the Liberal party in that division and be would rather be one of the vice-presidents. —lt was subsequently unanimously decided that Mr Joseph Evans, JP, of Haydock, should be the president, and the following gentlemen were elected vice-presidents :—Mr Charles Pilkingtoo, J P (Haydock) ; Mr William Mit- chell (aolborne) ; Mr Rawlins (Rainhill) ; Mr A C Mc- Corquotile, JP (Newten) ; Mr 8 Wools (Ashton-in. Makeifield) ; Mr Richard Pilkington, J P (Rainford) ; and Mr P Hall and Mr B Harrison (Earlestown). For the post of secretary Mr Thomas Howard, secretary of the Earles- town and District Liberal Club, and Mr Charles As'eton. of Earlestown, were nominated. Mr Howard Was elected by a large majerity. Mr P Hall, of Earlestown, was appoi fled treasurer. The Chairman afterwards observed that the members of the General Council would elect the proportion- ate share of delegates for each district on the Executive Council : and on the motion of Mr John Prescott, it was decided that a meeting of the Ex!cutive Council should Us held next week. SELECTION OF A CANDIDATE.

The Chairman then male are important announcement as to the Liberal candidate for the Newton division. He said he had been asked if there hod been anything done with regard to the selection of a candidate. He might perhaps make a statement in regard there to, but he hardly liked making it. A candidate had been spoken of generally about the township, and also in Liverpool, he believed. In New- ton, certainly, the name of Mr George McCorquodale had been pretty freely mentioned. (Applause.) Of course nothing could be done officially, simply because there was no one to do it. He (Mr Pilkington) had not been an officer of the Association, nor hod he any- thing to do with it, because it was not then formed ; but still for all that he went to Mr McCorquodale to get to know his feelings on the subj,mt. Mr McCorquodale said that he would very much prefer that if they could they should gel a better man than himself. He would rather work for some very well-knownmaan who might be selected. as a candidate than stand as a candidate himself, but if in the Liberal interest it was found that he was the best and most likely man to carry the constituency, then he thought, if his health permitted him, he should stand. (Applause.) At the same time that was not official, as the invitation for a candidate would have to first come from the Council. Mr. Roberts (Ashton) asked if it would not be advisable I for the Council to ask the chairman to request Colonel McCorquodale to attend the next meeting.—Mr. Prescott (garlestown) thought the Council should be gathered to- gether free and unfettered and then they could ccasider any other gentleman's qualifications who might be suggested as candidate.—Mr. Roberts said the Conservatives had already waited upon Sir Richard Cross. He did not think it was wise for the Liberals to waste time, for if they kept allowing week after week to go over their heads they would find that Sir Richard Cross had been elected.— The Chairman thought they were in advance of the Conservatives by the organisation they had formed. He thought the Executive should get to know the views of any candidates and afterwards bring them before a meeting of the General Council. They all knew what Mr McCor- quodale's ideas were, but there had been one or two other names mentioned, welch could be discussed at a future meeting.—After some discussion it was understood that the Executive should consider the names of several likely can- didates at their first meeting and submit one or two for the approval or selection of the General Council.

SUPFORT OF THE GOVERNMENT. The Chairman said he thought that was a fitting oppor- tunity to pass a vote of confidence in the Government. (Applause.) Though they had really met together for business purposes they ought to connect themselves with Liberalism all over the country.— Mr. William Evans, of Rainhill, said a vote of confidence from that meeting would strengthen any Government, for they must bear in mind that that meeting represented many thousands of persons throughout the Newton division. As a party he believed they could not find fault with Mr. Gladstone or his policy. They believed he was a man capable of leading them, and believing that they thought their representatives in the House of Commons should support him. (Applause.) He had great pleasure in proposing " That this meeting re- joices in the success which has attended the eforts of the Government to place representation of the people in the House of Commons on a democratic and sound basis, heartily approves of the present management of the nation's home affairs, and while deeply deploring the neces- sity for a military campaign in the Soudan, is of opinion that the general course of foreign policy which the Govern- ment has adopted amid exceptional circumstances, entitles it to the support of the Liberal party and the country. (Cheers.) He said they wore distinctly of opinion that the foreign policy of the Government had been safe, practicable, and honourable, and the action with regard to Afghanistan showed that they were not to be trifled with. (Applause.) —Mr S Woods, miners' agent, of Park-lane, Ashton. seconded the resolution in a stirring address. He said if they took into consideration the whole career of Mr Glad- stone he did not think they could find his equal if they searched the world through. While Mr Gladstone had never been a war man, he never was a peace- at-any-price man, but a peace-with-honour man, and be had consistently carried out that principle in every Govern- ment over which he had presided. If there was nothing else in the whole legislative career of Mr. Gladstone than what he had done during the year 1884 it ought to be suffi- cient to commend him to the working-men of the United Kingdom for the great amount of power which he had put in their hands, and which they ought to have had a century ago. The whole aim of Mr. Gladstone's policy had been to better the large bulk of the people of the country. (Ap- plause.) He thought his consistent action during the pre- sent Egyptian war and the Afghanistan question showed very distinctly that he was not wishful to shed life, to spend treasure, or do that which he knew must ultimately be a great scourge to the people. It was most unfair to throw the blame of the death of General Gordon on the shoulders of the present Government. (Applause.) The resolution was then enthusiastically carried, and the Chairman intimated that a copy would be sent to the Fame Minister.
On the motion of Mr Rawlins, seconded by Mr T Howard, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the chair- man, and the meeting concluded.

div.p: NO TES BY THE WAY.

_ The internattonal match played at Blackburn proved dis- appointing, and as on previous occasions on meeting the representatives of Wales the English eleven made a poor dis- play. On the Kennington Oval England beat Wales by two goals to one and five to none in 1879 and 1883 respectively, while at Wrexham in 1880 England won by three to two, and in 1884 by four to none, suffering defeat there in 1882 by five goals to three. Twice the Welshmen have been en- countered at Blackburn, and on the Alexandra Meadows they secured their first victory over England by one goal to none, while on Saturday the .first drawn game between the two nations was played. The aggregate score is now—Eng- land 18 goals, Wales 9; an average in favour of England by two goals to one.

The Glasgow Association have declined to arrange a match with Lancashire for next season, restricting their fixtnres to the associations of Sheffield, London, Birming- ham, and Edinburgh. On Saturday, Scotland beat Ireland, at Glasgow; at Der- by, Notts Forest and Queen's Park played a drawn game in the semi-final tie of the Association Cup competition ; at Bolton, the Wanderers beat Notts ; lialliwell beat Astlev Bridge; Great Lever beat Stoke ; West Bromwich Albion beat Aston Villa ; Westminster School beat OldWykehamists ; in the final tie of the Essex Cup competition, the Old For- esters beat Woodford Bridge; in a semi-final tie of the Bir- mingham Cup competition, Walsall Swifts beat ; Stavelev beat Sheffield Heeley ; in the semi-final tie of the Wharncliffe Charity Cup competition, Sheffield Wednesday beat Lockwood Bros., after a drawn game ; in the semi-final of the Sheffield Cup competition, Mexboro' and Park Grange failed to score.
