div.head: EAR LES TOWN.
div.p: EAR LES TOWN.

CONSERVATIVE CLUB BILLIARD HANDICAP.—During the present week there has been in progress at the Newton Polling Conservative Club, Earle-street, Earlestowo, a bil- liard handicap for the following prizes :-Ist, splendid cue and case and £1; 2nd, 15s ; 3rd and fourth, 5s each ; four prizes of 2s 6d each. The contest has excited considerable interest among the members, 64 of whom have entered their names as competitors. Goon TEMPLARY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day under the presidency of Bro. Joseph James, W.C.T. There was an excellent attendance. Bro. John Warburton read several circulars from the Grand Lodge, including one from the District Electoral Deputy dealing with electoral work, and the necessity for prompt and energetic action in the forthcoming parliamentary election. The programme for the evening was "Sharp practice," and impromptu ad- dresses were given on different subjects. CROW-LANE CATHOLIC CHAPEL.—In aid of the school funds an entertainment of an enjoyable character was given In St Mary's Catholic School, Crow-lane, on Tuesday even- ing. The principal feature was a representation of the at- tractive drama " The Chinese Mother." This piece has been lately given on two occasions in the same place, and on each occasion it was a great success. The last perfor- mance was no exception, there being a large and apprecia- tive audience. Selections of music were given by Mr Clyons, of Golborne' and Miss Riley, of Earlestown. GOSPEL MISSION CONCERT.—The Co-operative Hall was nicely filled on Saturday evening when a concert, under the conductorship of Mr fl J Darman, late organist of St John's Church, was given under the auspices of the Earles- town Gospel Mission. The proceeds were in aid of the har- monium fund, and there was a very large and interested audience. The vocalists were Miss Lewis, Miss Hard- man, Miss Davies, Mrs and Miss Walker, Miss Whitty, Miss Marsh, Mr Peter Hastie. Mr White' and Mr Barcroft, whose efihrts were highly appreciated. Selections of instru- mental music were given by Mr H McEleney (solo clarion- ette), Master B Tripp, Mr J Tripp, and Mr G Birks. A pianoforte solo by Miss Sudworth was nicely rendered. The choir splendidly sang several part songs. The accompanists were Mr H J Dursnan and Miss Sudworth. AN AMUSING CASE.—Before Messrs R Houghton, C Pilkington, and W F Gooch, at the Newton Town 11,11 on Saturday, Thomas Pill. of Earlestown, was summoned for being drunk at Earlestown on the 7th March —The de- fendant pleaded not guiltv.-I".C. Bunt st arid that on the Sate named he saw the defendant drunk. and incapable in Earle-street. He was in an empty potato hamper near a greengrocer's shop, and there Was nothing visible but his I legs. He asked witness to assist him out an I he did so. Witness ordered him away but the defendant returned.— The defendant denled that be was drunk, and asked if the officer could enter a priva e shop and turn him out when he isas sleeping. He called two witneeses named Edward Bradshaw and William Morris, who deposed that the den- dant was not drunk when they saw him about the time that had teen mentioned —The Bench remarked Oat there was a doubt in the case and it would be dismissed.

Tau EARLESTOWN BAND OF lEN—DNEZ.—The open- ing meeting in connectien with 'The General Earle Memo- rial" Branch of Kindness, recently established at Earles- town, took place in the Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School, Cross-lane, on Thursday evening, when there was a crowded attendance. Mr Charles Ashton presided, and he was sup- ported by "Uncle Gilbert " (Mr G R Kirlew, of Manches- ter)." Major" C Edwardes, of Liverpool ; " Lieutenant" Williamson, St. Helens ; and Mr John Roberts, Earle& town. The Chairman spoke very encouragingly of the workers in connection with the Band of Kindness, and ad- dresses were also given by the gentlemen named. An ex- cellently arranged programme of songs, recitations, etc., was gone through by Miss Sydes, Miss C B Roberts, Miss Louisa Seddon, Miss A Jackson, Miss A. Stringer ; Messrs Corlett, Roberts, and T W Stanfield. Miss Williams pre- sided at the pianoforte. The proceedings were of a very enjoyable character. LEITER FROM MR. W. E. GrAnsroNE.—On Thursday week, a meeting of the Liberals of Earlestown and district was held at the Co-operative Hall for the purpose of electing 69 representatives to serve on the Gefieral Council of the "300" for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire. At the same meeting a vote of confidence was passed in Mr. Gladstone and Her Majesty's present Government, and a copy was directed to be forwarded to the Prime Minister. This has been done, and the following communi- cation has been received in reply:—" 10, Downing-street, Whitehall. 18± March, 1885 —Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Gladstone to inform you that be has received the communi- cation which you have done him the honour to send him, and to convey to you his thanks for the expression of approval and confidence in Her Majesty's Government which it contains.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, H. W. Pant- ROSE.—Mr. T. Howard, secretary, Liberal Association, New- ton Division of South-West Lancashire." A. NEWTON IRISHMAN AND HIS "TROUSERS BRE/CORES." , —Roars of laughter were occasioned at the Newton Petty ' Sessions on Saturday, daring the heating of a summons against Martin Cassidy, of Newton, for being drunk and dls- orderly on the Bth inst. The magistrates on the Bench were Messrs R Houghton, C Pilkington, and W F Gooch. One of the witnesses was Police-sergeant Coramins, who spoke to having seen the defendant under the influence of drink, and be ordered the defendant home.—The defendant: Now was it you or your dog that spoke to me first? (Loud laughter.)—The Clerk: He will very likely say it was the dog.—The defendant: Yes, it was the dog—it ran at me.— The Clerk: We might call the doe as a witness 7—Defen• dent : Yes, the dog might be brought.—A little later the de- fendant asked: Did not the dog run very savage at me?— P.S. Commins : No.—Defendant: It ran and tried to bite my legs or my trousers breeches. (Loud laughter.)—Toe Chairman asked the defendant how often he had been before the Bench.—The defendant : I cannot tell you, sir.—The Chairman: It is so many. I will refresh your memory—it is 22 times. You must pay a fine of 51 and costs.

BRRACII OF FACTORY AND WORKSHOPS ACT. —Thos. Pope, a blacksmith in Princes-street, Earlestown was sum- moned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs It Houghton, C Pilkington, and W F Gooch, for two offences under the Factory and Workshops Act. Mr W H Brewer, of Bolton, her Majesty's Inspector of factories for this district, who prosecuted, explained that the defendant was summoned for employing a young person without hav- ing obtained a medical certificate, and also for neglecting to enter into a register provided for the purpose, the name of the young person employed by him. On the 10th February he visited Mr Pope's workshop and found a boy named Wm Webster at work there. The boy told him he had been em- ployed there for some time. When he called for the regis- ter the last name found to have been entered was on the 18th April, 1879. He had previously cautioned Mr Pope for his irregularity in that respect.—The defendant said he had had no lads employed at his works since the date last mentioned in his register.—George Webster, a lad, was then called. He stated that he had been in the service of the de- fendant for about two months past. —The defendant stated that he had been several times to Dr Watkins's surgery to obtain a certificate of the lad's fitness for work, but he had not been able to see the doctor. He neglected entering the name of the lad in the register until he obtained the medi- cal certificate.—Mr W H Brewer : He ought not to start the boy before he entered his name in the register. He afterwards observed that the case had been brought because the defendant had waled them a great deal of trouble The Chairman : You are fined 103 and costs in each case. —The Defendant: I cannot pay, that is all.—The Clerk : Then you will have to go for fourteen days' the usual de- fault —The Defendant : All right, sir. RIDING ON Till& RAILWAY WITHOUT Tlffitirr.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Messrs It Hough- ton, C Pilkingten, and W F Gooch, Ann Kearns, a second- hand clothes dealer, residing at Wigan, was summoned for travelling in a carriage on the Louden and North-Western Railway Company, between Golborne and Newton Bridge without a ticket, on the 9th February; and she was also summoned for travelling in a carriage between Warrington and Wigan without a ticket, on the 11th February.—Defendant pleaded not guilty to the first charge, and guilty in the second case.—Mr Preston, of Lime-street station, ap- peared on behalf of the railway company, and stated that the defendant had been summoned on two offences He was at a loss to understand why she should plead not guilty to the ilest charge, because when charged with it by the ticket collector at Wigan she acknowledged having come by train. The circumstances of the first case were these. The guard saw :the woman at Newton Bridge enter the train, and the ticket collector at Wigan saw her amcngst the passen- gers. The policeman in the employ of the company after- wards taxed her with having come by train. She replied, "I did. The reason! told the ticket collector I had only come from Golborne instead of Newton Bride was because lam short of money. lam sorry for it, and I will pay you now, and I hope You will let it drop." She wait afterwards charged with having travelled between Warrington and Wigan without having previously paid her fare, and she admitted it, adding that she hoped the fare would be ac- cepted, and that she would not be exposed. He (Preeton) explained that the woman was a dealer in old clothes, and as such was in the habit of travelling about the country, and was well acquainted with the railway service—Evi- dence to the foregoieg effect was then given, and the Chair- man, addressing the defendant, said she was no novice in travelling, and she knew pretty well the ins and outs of railway travelling. She must pay a fine of 30s and costs in each case.

div.head: NEWTON PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION. Tag LIBERAL "300."
div.p: THE NEWTON PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION. Tag LIBERAL "300."

The first general meeting of the recently-elected Liberal Three Hundred for the Newton Division of South-West Lan- cashire was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening, when there was a very large attendance. The principal towships of the division were well represanted. The chair was occupied by Mr Charles Pilkington, J P, and among those present were the Rev James Allatt (Newton) and F N Shimmin (Earleatown) ; Messrs M Birkhead, G Appleton, P Hall (Earlestown), W Mitchell, John Davies, and R Yates (Go'borne) ; Rawlins (Rainhill), F A it Neill (Bold), H D Maitland (Rainhill), W Evans (Rainhill), Thomas Esberts (Ashton-in-Makerfield), E Beilby (Hay. dock), (ie.

The Chairman said they were met that evening under very happy circumstances. About a fortnight ago they had a small informal meeting of the leading Liberal associations of that part of the district, and it was determined at that meeting to ask the various townships which had been banded together by the Boundary Commissioners and placed in the Newton Division of South West Lancashire, to form a

div.head: WELSH MUSICAL FESTIVAL.
div.p: WELSH MUSICAL FESTIVAL.

The Welsh..inhabTtanii-olit—rle-s—to-w-n- and district held their annual festival on Saturday afternoon, in the Wes- leyan Day School, Cross-lane, kindly lent for the occasion by the trustees. Tea was partaken of in the lower school- room, and about 160 persons were present. At the subse- quent meeting the Rey. E. Lloyd, St. Helens, occupied the chair, and the conductor of the meeting was the Rev. J. 0. Williams, Liverpool. It had been announced that prizes would be offered for choral competitions, speaking, and re- citing, and the room was nicely tilled. The conductor, who is one of the most popular of Welsh epigrammatists, under the nom de plume of " Pedrogwyson," was the adjudicator on the essays, poetry, reading, &c. After the congregation had heartily sung a hymn, the Chai:man delivered an appro- priate address. Next on the programme was a Bardic address by Mr. R. 0. Roberts. of Earlestown. The prizes for the various competitions were awarded as follows: For the best poetry on " Time," Mr Thomas Williams, Ashton ; for reciting the 134th Psalm, Willie Pierce, Earles- town ; best rendering of the solo, " Dost thou remember the moon rising," the prize was awarded to Mr John Nor- ris, Ashton; in the choral competition, on the congregational tune, the" Old 50th," three choirs took part, namely, the Ashton choir, the'Stubshaw Cross choir, and the Earles- town Choral Union. The last-named was declared the win-; Tiers. Mr Morris Watkin, Earlestown, took the prize for the; explanation of Welsh-English words, and for the best im- promptu speech, Mr James Pierce, Earlestown, was sue.; cessful. An address was given by Mr Israel Jones, who re-, ferred to the patron saint, David, after which the audience' sang the chorus, "The land of my fathers," with that spirit which is characteristic of such Welsh gatherings. Mrs Evans, Stubshaw Cross, gained the prize for rendering the Welsh solo " Chwyfior, cadach gwyn." For the best his- torical essay on " John the Baptist," Mr Robert Williams, Earlestown, was the winner. Mr James Pierce, Earlestown, won another prize for the best explanation of uncommon

Welsh words. The chief chord competition of the evening was a prize to the choir that best rendered the anthem" 0 Lord, thou has searched me and known me." The Stubshaw Cross Glee Party, under the leadership of Mr Job Roberts, and the Earlestown Choral Union, under the conductorship of Mr John H Profitt, competed. Both choirs were declared to be of equal merit. A hearty vote of thanks was given to the president, conductor, and others, after which the meeting was brought to a close. ,

Widnes, e. poor in the township of Widnes, in the said Union, refuee to permit the said William Rock to inspect the said book." For the complaiaant there appeared Mr Walton, barrister„ of Liverpool, and Mr S H Hartley, who pleaded not guilty appeared in hie own defence. Mr Walton explained that the summons was Wien ot:t under the Union Assessment Committee Act, 1802, he me 11th section of which it was enacted that Assessment 'Corn. mittees should cause a minute of their proceedings to be en- tered in a book provided for that purpose, and such beok should at all times and seasons be open to the inspection of every person rated to the relief of the poor, without fee or bounty. If the clerk should refuse to permit any such person to inspect or copy any extract he should be liable to a penalty not exceeding £5. The allegation was that Mr. Hartley re- fused to permit Mr. Rock, a ratepayer at Widnes, to inspect the minute book of the Assessment Committee. Mr. Rock was an accountant, sad on the 6th February he attended the offices of the Prescot Union at Whiston, for the purpose of of inspecting certain books relating to the union accounts. That day was a Friday, and the audit of the union accounts was to take place on the following Monday, and he wished to inspect the books with the view of raising certain questions before the auditor. Mr. Rock was at Mr. Hartley's office for a considerable time, and he asked to see the minute book. Mr. Hartley said he had no right to see it, and ab- solutely refused to let Mr. Rock see it. Mr. Hartley gave no other reason beyond that, but the Act stated distinctly that any ratepayer should be at liberty at all Cram to inspect it. That was a right given by the statute to the ratepayers for their own protection, and it was a right which was of special importance should be exercised. Mr. Rock was no doubt investigating the accounts of the unicn, and possibly Mr. Hartley looked upon him as a busy body ; but the pro- ceedings had not been brought with a view of inflating a penalty upon Mr. Hartley but simply in order to assert the right which Mr. Rock as well as every ratepayer bad to see the book at any seasonable time. As far as he (Mr. Walton) was concerned he wished to obtain a declaration from the Bench as to the rights of the rateDayers.—William Rock. the complainant, was then called, lie deposed that he was a chartered accountant at Widnes, and was a ratepayer in the Prescot Union. For certain reasons he was looking into the accounts of the Union, and on the 13th February he attended the Union offices at Whieton, where he saw Mr Hartley. He asked Mr Hartley if he would produce the minute book of the Assessment Committee, but he declined to do so, and said he would decline to discuss the matter. He remained at Mr Hartley's office from eleven o'clock in the forenoon until six or seven o'clock in the evening.—In reply to Mr Hartley, complainant said he did not ask for another minute book beyond the minute book cf the Assess- ment Committee. He did not ask for the minute book of the Guardians. He had subsequently asked for certain vouchers. On the first day of the audit he did not com- plain to the auditor that certain books had not been pro- duced.—Mr Hartley: Who paid you for attending my audit P—Mr Rock: I will answer the question if you like.— Mr Walton: Is this necessary P—Mr Rock: No one was paying me.—ln reply to further questions, the complainant said he did nOtflay anything to the effect that he would not have come as a professional rnan if he was not being paid. He did not lead the defendant to believe that he (complainant) was being paid by Messrs Gaskell, Deacon and Co., of Widnes. He was not acting for that firm. He was acting as a ratepayer, .and for himself. He had not charged anybody for his time.—Mr Walton: I think these questions ought not to be raised.—Mr Hartley: I want to prove that his word cannot be relied upon—that when he tells me one thing he tells something different to others. Mr. Hartley submitted that no demand bed been ever made to him by Mr Rock to produce the minute book of the Assessment Committee. On the Friday that Mr Rock called the chairman of the Board of Guardians was present and heard the conversation that took place, and he would say that he never heard the minute book of the Assessment Committee asked for. The minute book of the Guardians, vouchers, and other things were asked for, and it had been the invariable custom of the office to produce what was asked for in a proper manner. Mr Rock never applied for the book to which he had alluded, and that was his (Mr Hartley's) answer to the case. He also maintained that Mr Rock had asked for the book at an unseasonable time; and he also maintained that Mr Rock did not appear as a rate. payer, but on behalf of Messrs Gaskell, Deacon, and Cone- pany.—Mr J T Hall, chairman of the Prescot Board of Guardians, said he was present in Mr Hartley's race when Mr Rock was there. Mr Rock asked the defendant to pro- duce the minute hook of the Guardians and some vouchers. He did not hear the complainant say anything about the Assessment Committee's minute book. —By Mr. Walton: Witness was signing documents when the conversation took place.—Mr. William Davies, a clerk in Mr Hartley's office, said repeated applications hid been made for the minute books.—Mr Walton : Has this , anything to do with the case P—Mr Hartley :I am showing what the practice of the office has been.—Mr Walton : The practice of the office has nothing to do with it. The ques- tion is whether Mr Hartley was asked to produce lbe book, and whether he refused.—The witness said Mr Rock did not ask him for the minute book of the Assessment Committee. —Mr Walton : Mr Rock did not say that he did ask you. —The Chairman : The case is dismiesed.—Mr Hartley asked for an order for the costs.—The Bench could not grant the costs as they thought it was a proper case to bring before the court to be inquired into.

They did not very often give dinner parties, says a con- temporary, and never gave large ones; but at the little reunions to which they did invite their friends they liked everything of the beet. So, on the afternoon of one of their choice little feasts, the host summoned his boy in buttons, and said, "Now, John, you must be very careful how you hand round the wine." "Yes, sir." "These bottles with the black seal are the best, and these with the red seal the Inferior sherry. 'The best sherry is for after dinner; the inferior sherry you will hand round with the hook after soup. You understand—hock and the inferior sherry after soup?" "Yes, sir, perfectly," said the boy in buttoss. And the evening came, and the guests came, and everything was progressing admirably till the boy went round the table asking of every guest, "Hock or inferior sherry 1' Every- body took hock. LEGAL PHEASEOLOGY.—It a man would, according to law, give to another an orange, instead of saying "I give you that orange "—which one would think would be what is called in legal phraseology " an absolute conveyance of all right and title therein "—the phrase would ran thus—" I give you all and singular my estate and interest, right, title, and claim, and advantage of and in that orange with all its rind, skin, juice, pulp, and pips, and all right and advantage therein, with full power to bite, cut, suck, and otherwise eat the same, or give the same away, as fully and effectually as I, said the A. 8., am now entitled to bite, cat, suck, or otherwise I eat the said orange, or give the same away with or without Its rind, juice, pulp, and pips, anything heretofore or here- after, or in any other deed or deeds, instrument or instru- ments of what nature or kind soever to the contrary in any wise notwithstanding." Mr. Greville, the late Clerk to the Privy Council, was persuaded, when he was over sixty years of age, to attend a spiritualistic séance. Foster, the presiding medium, was in great form, and the revelations were astounding. Greville sat silent, and his aged wizened f ace was emotionless as a mask. Suddenly the medium grew excited, and said to the old gentleman, "A female form is bending over you. Oh, the extraordinary likeness !" Greville sighed. "She lifts her hands to bless you." Greville sighed again. "It is your mother !" " Ah, poor thing," said Greville; "I'm glad !" "She smiles! She says all is well with her !" Greville sighed again, and said, "I'm delighted !" "She says she will see you soon. You are old, and you must meet her before long." Then Greville quietly observed, "That's very true! I'm going to take tea with her at five o'clock this evening." Tableau! His mother was then, though ninety years old, hale and vigorous. How lam ACCOUNT was SICTTLED.—Among the disci- plinary advantages of Eton College was, and still is, that of being birched. About this performance Mr. Payn, in his recent book, tells one of his capital stories. "A. humorous lad I will call Vivian, who had reached the rather unflog- gable age of seventeen, and was on the point of entering the Army, was 'swished," as he thought unjustly, the very , week before his departure from the school. In those days a perquisite—and a very large perquisite—of the head-master's was a ten-pound note given to him by every fifth-form boy on leaving. The etiquette was to call at the lodge and drop the note into a jar, or anything handy, where the doctor could find it after his dear pupil had gone away. It was something like the visit of a delicate minded patient to a doctor of medicine. But Vivian only pretended to drop his ten-pound note into the jar, and reserved it for more agreeable purposes. He pictured to himself with great satisfaction the head-master's fruitless hunt after that bit of tissue-paper, after he had got over the emotion of wishing him farewell. 'I can't flog him for flogging me unjustly,' was his reflec- tion; but, dash it, I can fine him!'"

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON. Tat:tamer. There is a page in the Times to which it may be pre- sumed that Mr. Ashmead Bartlett and gentlemen of his per- suasion first turn when the paper first reaches them. This is the fifth page, and it occurs to one in glancing over it this morning that it must be instructive reading for the Jingo party, which is now attempting to raise its head after the terrible beating it got at the general election of 1880. According to these authorities Mr. Gladstone's Government has brought the name of England into contempt and die- repute. From St. Petersburg to Lisbon, from Constanti- nople to Paris the name of England is a by-word. In India the natives are only waiting for an opportunity to revoltil whilst such has been the conduct of colonial affairs that there is not a colony which is not estranged. Now let ii look at the Times, itself the principal organ of the doctrine preached in the House of Commons and through the cos& try by Mr. Ashmead Bartlett. The first telegram is from Vienna and calls attention to the fact that " the tone of the Russian press has changed greatly within the last few days. IFriendly language is now being need towards England, ' whilst the tone towards Germany is bitter." " It is thought in Vienna," the correspondent adds, " that the visit of the Prince of Wales to Berlin must tend to convince the Rus- sians still further of their interest in keeping on good terms with England." From Rome there is telegraphed a digest of the meeting if the Chamber of Deputies, in which Signor Bovio, speak- ing in the name of the Extreme Left, expresses satisfaction at the closer relations established with England, " who," he said," would be far more useful and friendly to Italy than the Central Powers would be." Another deputy, approach- ing the subject from a different political section 13" anxious above all things that an understanding should be established with England." Every member who speaks makes the relations with England the principlal object of his remarks, whilst the Prime Minister elicits general cheering by his declaration that" Italy's friendship with England is of the warmest character." Frem Berlin is continued the series, prolonged through several days, of expressions of satisfac- tion et tho entablialarnont nf better relations with England. From Constantinople it is reported that " the local prints known to derive their inspiration from the Palace, pointedly remark on the advantages of a British alliance." From Paris there are expressions of French jealousy at the new relations of England with Germany testifying to the im- portance of the British alliance; whilst from New South Wales there is a reference to the departure of the contingent for Suakim the outward and visible sign of those relations with the colenies which have yielded fruit in the offers of material assistance, which at once places England in the very front rank of the military Powers in the world. But these are all hard facts, and gentlemen of whom Mr. Ash- mead Bartlett is the type, are not affected one way.or the other by so base an influence as facts. Parliament, or rather the House of Commons, has bad a busy week. The Lords come as usual at four o'clock, and depart as customary between five and six, having in that meantime saved the nation without imperilling their own' dinner. Foreign aff -ars have largely occupied the attention of the Commons. Mr. Ashmead Bartlett has been more active than ever. New Guinea, which he was recently dis- posed to take up, is quite neglected, his attention being riveted upon Afghanistan and the many iniquities of her Majesty's Government in that direction. Indeed, it is ques- tionable whether in taking up New Guinea he was animated by any other idea than that of keeping off Sir Henry Tyler, who has displayed a sudden access of activity in the field hitherto appropriated by the member for Eye. Mr. Bartlett. has here acted after the manner of the German Government in their colonization policy. Ile has stuck up his flag on New Guinea not because he has anything particular to say about it just now, but to keep others off the ground. It is a significant fact that the Conservative party are now and at last beginning to recognise Mr. Ashmead-Bart- lett. Hitherto they have been inclined to join in the con- tumely with which his constant uprising is received frJrn the Liberal Benches. But lately he has been cheered when proposing to supplement a question by one or two others. This is generally construed as a rebuke for Sir Stafford Northcote. If he will not at a serious crisis worry the Government with inconvenient questions they can only mutter complaints. But if a directly different course is taken by a member, however inconsiderable, they can cheer him, and so, by implication, rebuke their Leader. The Oppogition is just now suffering from an access of disorgauisation. This has been brought to a head by the al of their leaders in the matter of the Redistribution Bill. A certain compact was made to which Lord Salisbury and Sir S. Northcote were parties, and which, being com- municated to the Conservative party, received their ap- proval. The leaders feel themselves bound to carry out the understanding, even on points wherein it will operate to their political disadvantage. But such is the standard of morality established among an important section of the Conserva- tive party, that on this point an open split arises. "Take whatever you can get as your share of the bargain," Con- servative gentlemen say to their leaders ; " but when it comes to your fulfilling your engagements, bluntly refuse, and do everything in your power to prevent them being carried out." Sir S. Northcote, it need hardly be said, do. dined to take that view of his duty. He voted with the Government in support of clauses which were not to his political taste, rine found himself, as he complained at the meeting of the Conservative party held at the Carlton Club on Monday, almost alone in the lobby. This happened on two important occasions, a repetition which proved too much even for the long suffering of Sir Stafford Nertbcote. He summoned a meeting of the party, at which, it was be- lieved in some quarters, he intended to place his resigns. tion in the hands of a body of gentlemen who had dire. owed and had attempted to dishonour him. But Sir Stafford Northcote is not food of extreme measures. He was content with mildly protesting, and having been himself severely lectured, the meeting separated. How long this state of things can endure it is not easy to say, but one would imagine the time could not be long. his a long time since so many notable trials took place within such narrow limits of time as has marked the present epoch. There was the Durham nullity suit which for nearly a week formed part of the breakfast faro of the country. This has been followed within the last few days by two libel suite against the World, the Bhabba case, and last but not least the charge against Mr. Hoare. In this last, as in the Durham Case, people moving in the higher classes of society are immediately concerned, and what has been made known in open court of their manner of proceed- ing is not likely to raise society in the Victorian age in the estimation of posterity. Almost the only respectable per- son who appears in the cue is the girl who was wronged. Mr. Justice Chitty ia giving judgment, alluded to what he called "the startling fact" of the girl's parents begging three thousand pounds from Mr. Hoare as" unwise and in- judicious," which is perhaps on the whole not too strong a way of putting it. Miss Sumner is, 1 believe, the grand- daughter of a former archbishop of Canterbury. Mr. Biggar is in high spirits on the Eastern Question. He is, by rare distinction among his party, a monied man, and it appears that he had placed a sum of £2,000 in Rus- sian Bonds. On the very day before the fall took place Mr. Biggar, withdrawing for a moment his attention from paro- chial affairs in Ireland, focussed it upon the probability of affairs In Afghanistan, and decided to sell out. This he did, and the next day the Bonds went down three per cent. Mr. Biggar was naturally pleased, and did not hide his satis- faction, more especially in the presence of holders of the stock who were less fortunate than himself. But it did not modify his implacable attitude towards the Government, and through the two all-night sittings which have marked the course of the Parliamentary week Joseph Gillis has been prominent for the pertinacity of his obstruction. The picture season now coming on is not regarded by the Painters with high hope. There are some men, like Millais, Sir Frederick Leighton, and, of late years, Frank Roll, who still get their prices, princely as they are. It is the rank and file of the profession that feel the pinch. People who had money to buy pictures seem to have covered their walls, and no one is coming forward to occupy their places. There is no profession that is influenced more closely by the ebb and flow of trade than that of the artists. The nouveaux riches always buy pictures, and like to pay a big price for them. They do not know anything about art, but feel con- tent if they get a large or small coloured canvas nicely framed with an incontestable signature of a fashionable painter, and they are prepared to pay for it. But the nouveaux riches seem to be an extinct species, like the dodo, and painters sorely complain. Mr. Agnew, perhaps the highest authority on the subject, whilst speaking of the existing depression in the picture trade, tells me it is likely to be much worse before it mends. The theatres are all preparing for the Easter campaign. There is a general change of programme In the wind. The Savoy has, in fact, begun. I think there has been more gush about this Japanese opera than about any of the other Gilbert-Sullivan productions. As a rule, Mr. Gilbert is very reticent. He likes hie surprises to be surprises, but this time he took the public into his confidence and told them what his plot would be. The success of a first night does not really count for very much. The test will be in ten days to come. lam going to be courageous, and will say that the mole is not quite up to the mark, but that the acting is far beyond it. Mr. Gilbert has worked very hard, and his work bears fruit. On other boards pieces are run- ning flatly to their dreary end. I don't think the Kendals will again try Shakeapeare. They are so perfect in modern characters that blank verse and Elizebethian poetry puts them oat. The Queen's Shilling is really one of the best things Mr. Kendal does. There in reason for all this activity. The great enemy of the theatre has put forward its announcement also. In the first week in May the Inventories will open at South Ken sington, and if we haves warm spring the theatres will feel it. The Omnibus Company has already made its prepara- tions for the event, end has pat on an almost perfect set of vehicles, and reduced, or at least apportioned, its fares. Bad' days seem in store for the theatre interest. Perhaps the Bancrofts were wise to retire.

It would next cross the mouth of the river Weaver, and pass In' front of the docks at Weston Point and Runcorn, until the bridge of the London and North-Western Railway was reached. The spans of this bridge, which were on fiat girders, were 300 feet in width, and the canal would absorb one half of the Cheshire span. It would pass in front of the docks of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation Company, and at thatpoint the Ship Canal commenced. At Eastbam there would be a group of tidal locks of the same size as those in the upper navigation. These locks would be tidal, and the ordinary navigation would be carried on with the gates open. Embankments would be constructed wherever the canal was carried along the foreshore, and these embankments would have at various points 48 tidal opening', each 100 feet wide. These were to admit the tide flowing in an out of the canal without interruption. The upper surface of the embankment would be 9ft. above high spring tide, which Would prevent the waves in rough weather affecting the Ship Canal, and stop the wasting of the shore, with the consequent increase of the sand banks in the estuary. The land waters would have free passage into the estuary as at present, and the land drainage generally would not be affected. The Marquis of Cholmondeley, who would be most seriously affected, had approved the plans in this respect. The lines beyond which town dues could not be collected by the Liverpool authorities extended from Beath= Ferry to a point opposite Garstoa, and the entrance to the canal would thus be exclu- ded from the operation of the dues. Mr Williams described, by reference to a large-sized model, the plan which would be adopted for carrying the canal across the mouth of the Weaver, and said they could be done with per- fect success, and without interference with the navigation of the Weaver er the ship canal. The Weaver traffic was becoming more and more steam traffic, and this would not be at all affected, though the promoters pledged themselves to provide power to assist sailing craft whenever necessary. The total length of the canal would be 34 miles 7 furlongs. From Eastharn to Latchford would be 20 miles 6 furlongs, and the remaining portion of the canal would be inland. There would be four locks on the canal, and these would be constructed in accordance with plans submitted when the Bill was first deposited. It was well known that the Irwell was a dark river—(a laugh)—but, owing to the action of the local authorities stimulated by the Rivers Pollution Act, the quality of the water is improving, and there coald be no objection to the canal on that score. It was proposed to pump water into the docks from wells in the red sandstone. The serious floods which periodically visited the districts would be confined within the banks of the canal, and the landlords and tenants on the banks would reap the benefit without any rate being levied on them. The speed of the steamers using the canal would be about five miles an hour, and the journey from 'b' mouth of the canal to the docks at Manchester would occupy about eight hours, allowing ample time for the passage of the locks; but it would be possible to ac- complish the distance in less time. From the canal there , k would be direct communication with the entire inland canal . system of the district. SOCIALISM AND NATIONAL SOBRIETY.

Sir,—Under the above heading the Rev. G. S. Reamey writes in To-Day a very impressive article. Various argu- ments have from time to time been pat forward, with the view of convincing the people generally—but more especi- ally the working-men—of the great and argent necessity for more moderation, or for complete abstinence. I know of none that strike with such force as the article now under notice. It needs no apology for introducing Mr. Reaney to the notice of your readers. While residing in Warriegton he made himself acquainted with the life of its workers ; in London amongst the Socialists and the poor of the East end, his name is becoming a household word. lam pleased to have the opportunity of saying that the present time seems to be somewnat remarkable as being seized bold of by men of the "cloth" and turned to some advantage. In various towns lectures of a striking character are being given, and Warrington in a somewhat accidental fashion gets a little of the benefit. Thanks to the Rev. Morley Stevenson and the Co-operative Society, we have just had a visit from the , II Rev. W. Tuekwell, and those who heard his splendid lecture 1 entitled " Utopia," will, I think, remember the name should the gentleman again honour Warrington with a visit. "Utopia "or shall! say England in a huadred years from now? Thiele a vast subject, Mr. Editor, yet who shall say the rev, gentleman's dream may not become a reality ? How is it to be done? Which way shall we set about it ? First, we mast insist upon men like the Rev. E. C. E. Carleteu being cleared out of the way. They block the road, strongly imbued as they are with antiquated Conservative notions. We never find them on the side of progress; dreaming of a past that gave them power, they dread look- ing into that future, so full of hope and promise for the people. Who can point eat in Warrington a Radical par- son, one who dare, or can, take the platform, and invite the people's confidence? None such exists. Having done this, the foremost question becomes the great and all-important one, How shell we promote sobriety amongst the people? I must not be understood as writing sa a total abstainer. At present I have no sympathy with their modes of procedure. Temperate on the drink question, they are intemperate in their language, consequently teetotallers repel the people. We all know how stringent laws in the past failed. Sump- tuary laws were adopted with the view of controlling and guiding the people in their worship of the goddess fashion. Criminal laws in the good old ages were of so vengeful a character that crime grew instead of decreasing; so we may venture to assert would the drinking habits of the people if repressive measures were adopted. Quite otherwise will it belt we take the people by the hand, and unknown to them- selves lead them out of the baneful habits that attend their intemperate lives. It needs no extra amount of exertion on the part of anyone to realise the fearful amount of intem- perance there is going on amongst the people, and I am convinced that this evil does not by any means lie solely to the working-men's charge. The upper and middle classes are its victims to a degree that is little understood by those who provide the means. But it is net with these! have to do; they will sooa find their senses when the working-man once appreciates the exact positiou of things. Mr. Reaney says—" Drink is the resource of thousands in their sorrow and their joy. It intrudes with most pernicious effect into our workshops and places of trade." This is the sad truth ; the habit so controls the working-man that he cares not to look about for the outcome of it all, and yet the result of this drinking habit is the one thing that be is daily fighting against., that is, the power that accumulating capital gives to his employer. To the wage earner the question of greatest importance is the amount received for labour given; and yet take the brewing trade, in which the wage earner re- ceives the smallest pittance, and look at the brewers them- selves. The slightest glance at the two great local brewing firms should be enough to convince anyone that the welfare of the people is never for one moment considered, nor yet can anyone say that out of the thousands yearly drained Out of Warrington does even the slightest pittance find its way back to benefit those already injured by its loss. Sir A. B. Walker in Liverpool raises art galleries, that future inhabitants of Utopia will look to as monuments of , a past age's idiocy. It would be interesting to know how many churches and chapels owe their existence to the well filled purses of capitalist brewers. Mr. Reaney says The wealth of brewers, like their piety, is almost a proverb, only the one is much more real than the other." Do we ever cm- eider what must be the power of wealthy, and, as a rule, unprincipled brewers in a small town ? Why, it is no se- cret that numbers of tradesmen could a tale unfold of the cringing and bowing done in the past, of the relief at present felt, and a dread lest a mistaken confidence of the working- man in a future Toryism should bring him face to face with the man who disfigures every street corner with a hell trap, baited with the working-man's bane. Socialists are to-day fighting with Capital. They anxiously desire the help of all. I have no hesitation in saying Mr. Reaney is right in his assertion that " There are associated with the drink trade such a mass and variety of evils that the mere enumeration of them is literally appalling." In every town and village no doubt can exist that the biggest half of the distress existing is associated with excessive drinking. Crime is in nearly all cases mixed up with it. The money r Spent on it by workmen would in a very short time enable , them to take their rightful places in the labour world. There is never a labour dispute without the accompsnying Imischief brought about by too much time being spent at the " pub." A great evil of this love of the public-house Is that no time is given for self-improvement. I wonder how many workmen in this town have read the book referred to by Mr. Tuckwell, "Utopia." a shilling book containing hints for solving the social problem, and worth twelve month' self•denial by every working-mau. Mr. Roney

LEADER WILLIAMS, engineer of the scheme, further examined by Mr. Michael, Q.C., said that if the canal now proposed were made, great benefit would result ,to the estuary by preventing the erosion of the banks I which was new going on. From his experience, he could not see how the working expenses of the canal would ex- ceed 15 per cent. The maintenance of a canal was not a very expensive matter, lie denied that the dredging at Run- corn bridge could interfere with the safety of that struc- ture, and said there was no allegation for the petition of the London and North-Western Company that the works would tend to silt up the entrance to the port at Garston. There would be no interference with the tidal waters which would affect either the estuary or the Bridgewater Canal. The Mersey and Irwell Navigation had recently commenced works of their own. In Man- chester the general impression not unfairly was that it was an attempt to increase to the promoters of the Ship Canal the price of the property of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, which they would have to purchase.—Cross- examined by Mr. Bidder, Q.C., who, with Mr. Aspinall, Q C., appeared for the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board, Mr. WILLIAMS said this very scheme was one of the schemes considered by him in the origin of the Ship Canal move-

ment, but he abandoned it, though he had never changed I his opinion that the use of training walls similar to those successfully used on the Tees is the proper way to do the work.—ln answer to Mr. Saunders, Q.C., who appeared for the Bridgewater Canal Company, witness thought it a little strange that that company, after agreeing with the promo- ters for two years,should sow be rushing forward with works a their own.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

The cross•examination of Mr. Leader-Williams, engineer o the scheme, was continued by Mr. Saunders on behalf of the Bridgewater Canal Company. Last year the Widnes people were very anxious that the ship canal should go on their side of the river, and they were deeply disappointed that the promoters now proposed to go down on the Bridge- water Canal side. The excavations just above Widnes would not affect the entrance to the Bridgewater Canal, and he did not think any of the canal works would interfere with the regime of the estuary. Both the ship canal promoters and the Bridgewater Canal Company would navigate the same water near Runcorn and at certain states of the tide a sort of preference would be given to the Bridgewater boats. He understood from the remarks made at the annual meeting of the Bridgewater Canal Company that the revenue had diminished last year.— Mr. Ledgard cross-examined the witness on behalf of the Weaver Navigation Company. List year the proposed ' canal interfered absolutely with the trade of the Weaver, and the promoters gave them 'free user," but the scheme of this year would not so interfere. Witness further said that he was prepared to advise the promoters to give tbe same priority of traffic over the Ship Canal to the Weaver Navigation that would be given to the Bridgewater Naviga- tion. .

THURSDAY. Mr. Leader-Williams was further cross-examined by Mr. Littler with reference to the cue of Sir Humphrey de Traf- ford. He said he considered that Sir Humphrey was en. titled to have frontage to the park side of the canal to de- velope it as he pleased, subject to his not interfering with the traffic of the canal. The witness was next cross- examined by Mr. Edge on behalf of Mr. Thomas Chadwick, of the Ordsall Paper Works Manchester. Cross-examined by Mr. Pope for the London and North-Western Railway Company, be said he did not consider the scheme could in any way affect Garston, and, indeed, he believed it would be a good.: thing for the railway company. He did not propose to bring the deep water up to Eastharn, but only to dredge a channel deep enough to give access to the canal. He was aware that nothing would please the London and North-Western Company. Re-examined . With reference to the works at Runcorn Bridge, they were to be carried out simply to compensate for the space which the canal would occupy there, and so that the channel should in no way be interfered with or the flow of the water into the estuary be altered. No new chan- nel would be created by those works.—Mr. horns ABER- NETHY, CE, was next called and examined by Mr. Michael. He said he approved of the schemes of 1883 and 1884; but, as they were rejected, he gave his attention to another route, which should not interfere with the estuary, and should leave the port of Liverpool and Garston uninjured. For that purpose he examined both sides of the estuary care- fully, and came to the conclusion that the work could be I carried out on the Cheshire side of the estuary without ia- jury to anyone, an outlet being given at Eastham. In his opinion the canal would form a protection to all the existing works on the south side of the estuary.—Mr. G. E. HILL, CE., said he was well acquainted with the Mersey, and considered that the present scheme was altogether outside of the estuary and could have no effect upon it, all the points which influenced the currents being left un- touched.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

A Cabinet Council was held in Downing-street at two o'clock on Friday. All the Ministers were present except Earl Spencer. Tke Admiralty received a telegram on Friday, stating that the hired transport Horsley, No. 40, previously re- ported as disabled, had passed Gibraltar, for Suakim. Viscount Ebrington addresrod a Liberal meeting Mat Tavistock, on Friday. He was afterwards unanimously selected candidate for the Tavisteck Division, Devonshire. The Central News understands that immediately after the recess a la,ge representative meeting will be held in the City of London to consider the condition of the Royal Navy. I The Cork Corporation on Friday declined to present 'an address to the Prince and Princess of Wales on the 'loyal visit, resolving to adopt an attitude of respectful neutrality. Samna AT ROCIIDALE.—On Friday morning, about nine o'clock, a stranger, attired as a working-man, was seen by ' Jebn Collier, mechanic, to jump into the reservoir con- nected with the paper works at Belfleld, Rochdale. He gave an alarm, and an attempt was made to rescue the man, but the water being very deep, he was not got out until life was extinct.

FRANCE AND CHINA.—PEACE NEGOTIATIONS. The St. James's Gazette is informed that the Chinese Minister in Berlin has received an intimation from the , French Government to the effect that it would be desirable ,to resume peace negotiations. The Chinese Minister, before I communicating with his Government, made it clearly under- stood that Chins would never consent to pay any war in- demnity, and negotiations would probably be resumed on , the basis of the cession of Tonquin to the French. It is not believed that China will consent to the temporary occupa- tion of Formosa. RICE AS CONTRABAND OF WAR. The Gazette publishes two notes addressed by M. Wad- dington to Earl Granville in regard to the French claim to treat rice as contraband of war. On the 24th M. Wadding- ton informed Earl Granville that the French Government had recognised the possibility of admitting in the in- terests of the commerce of neutrals an alleviation of the measure. Therefore shipment of rice destined for Canton and the southern Chinese ports would be allowed to pass freely from the 26th February. The shipment for Chinese ports north of Canton would alone be prohibited, ar.d treated as contraband of war.

THE SOTIDA:N CAMPAIGN. BATTLE NEAR SUAKIM. THE REBELS DEFEATED WITH GREAT LOSS. A Central News telegram, dated Souakim, Friday morn- ing says :—Nearly the whole of the British troops marched out of camp at seven o'clock this morning for the scene of veeterday's operations. It is believed something more seri- ous is intended to-day. Two days' rations have been taken, full water supply, and six Gardner guns. The rebels will probably make their stand among the hills and broken ground beyond Haeheen. A determined opposition is ex- pected. A second edition of the Daily Chronicle contains the foie lowing telegram :—Suakitn, Friday, 7-45 am. Our force started again at daylight this morning for Hasheen. It is believed that a liattle is imminent on the hills beyond that place. The troops have taken two days' rations and no less than 23,000 gallons et water. To-day the Gardner battery of six guns has been taken forward for the first time. The gene are drawn by mules. Captain Crooke, of the Marines, is in command of the artillery. The transport and commis- sariat arrangements on the march are under the direction of Captain Decosson. Stratum, FRIDAY Avrermorne.—Heavy firing is now going on beyond Hasheen. The rebels apparently hold the hills in force, and reply briskly to the British fire. The whole British force in front is engaged. &ARM, FRIDAY NIGHT.—The firing at the front con- tinued some hours, the Gardner guns playing havoc on the rebel ranks. The enemy, however, stood their ground well, I and it was not until late in the afternoon that they evacua- ted their positions on the hills. The rebel loss was very heavy. Our own casualties are not numerous. We now occupy the enemy's positions, and camp on the ground to- night. Further fighting is expected to-morrow, when our force will probably reach Tamai, the rebel stronghold. GENERAL GRAHAM'S DESPATCH. An official telegram from General Graham, dated Hasheen, Friday afternoon says the British force reached the wells at 8-20 this morning:The enemy retreated to the neigh- bouring bills. The Berkshire men and Marines cleared them off very effectively, the rebels retiring towards Tarnal. The j Indian Lancers charged them and the guns opened fire upon them. The sth Lancers charged the rebels on the right. An entrenched camp is now being formed. Captain Dallison (Scots Guards), Sergeant-Major Nicholls (sth Lancers), and seven men are killed. Surgeon-Major Lane, Major Harvey (sth Lancers), Major Robertson (9th Bengal Cavalry), and 36 men are wounded. The enemy's estimated strength is , four thousand. MOVEMENTS ON THE NILE. A Central News telegram dated Korti, Friday morning, , states :—The prospects of fighting on the Nile are not yet over. The Mudir, who is about a dozen miles beyond Merawi' is preparing for an onslaught upon the rebel posi- tions. He has recruited the Khabba.,ish and the Shayryeh tribes of Arabs, and, besides these, he has nearly a thousand trained Egyptian soldiers with four guns. He will make a raid upon the rebel post of Hassamvet first of all, but it is reported on apparently good ground that his operations will not be confined to that quarter alone, and that a much more adventurous scheme is in contemplation. According to the latest information received here, the Mandi is still in the vicinity of Khartoum, having taken up his quarters at I Omdurman. The third edition of the Daily Chronicle contains a sum- mary of a long dispatch which reached it this morning from its special correspondent at Korti, stating that the Mudir of Dongola is about to attack the rebels at Hassani- i yet. It is reported that he will afterwards, if successful, move upon Berber. He has Egyptian soldiers with him, 'three guns, and one Gaffing. The Khabbabish and Shay- ! iyeh tribes have joined him. The Mudir is now twelve miles above Merawi. KORTI, FRIDAY.—A large convoy of sick were sent down the Nile to-day in a yarrow-stern wheel boat. THE LATE GENERAL STEWART.

Lord Wo'matey, in notifying to the War Office the death of General Sir Herbert Stewart, says few commanders have succeeded in winning to such an extent the affection of those who served with or under him. His many high military qualities rendered him a General whom England could ill afford to spare. Leaders such as he are rare in all armies; it may be long before the service or the country , can fill the gap his death has caused.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIA.MENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Fnthay. The House met at four o'clock. Miscamaxxons.—Earl DILLANERE gave notice to ask the Foreign Secretary whether the French Government had expressed a desire to have co-operation in Tunis of a power less antagonistic than Turkey, and whether undertaking existed between England and Turkey in reference to the Mediterranean shores of Turkey.—Earl GRANvir-tn stated that on Friday next the House would adjourn until the 13th April.

TRW-SUNDAY QIIESTION.—Lord THURLOW moved a reso- lution in favour of opening museums on Sundays. , Earl CAIRNS, for Lord Salisbury, moved a negative amendment.—Lord Bramwell, Lord Mount Temple, and Earl Cowper supported the reso- lution in favour of the Sunday opening of the museum.— The Earl of Harrowby and the Archbishop of Canterbury opposed it —Earl GRANVILLE said the Government had not thought it right to interfere in a social question, the decision of which rested with public feeling. Personally he sup- ported the resolution.—The Duke of Argyle and Earl Den- bigh opposed, and the House divided—for the resolution 64; against 64.—The LORD CHANCELLOR decided that according to the rule of the House the resolution was re- jected.

Some minor business having been dispesed of, the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. THE SOLIDAN.—Mr ASIIMEAD BARTLETT gave notice that on an early day he would call attention to the great loss of life in the Soudan owing to the policy of her Majesty's Government, and move that the abandonment of the garrison of Kassala with 25,000 people there was a disgrace to the country and an outrage on humanity.—Mr. KYNAS. TON CROSS. replying to Dr Cameron, said offers that had been made to her Majesty of troops by Nizam of Hyderabad, had been suitably acknowledged. Lord FITZMAIIRICE, replying to Mr. Pulestone, said it was not, true that Lord Wolseley had been proposed as Gover- nortGcneral of the Soudan. FRANCE AND CHINA.—Lord E FITZMAXTRICE, replying to Mr Gorst, said the Government had recognised the right of search by the French Government of British vessels for contraband of war bound to Chinese ports and Hong Kong. He could not say whether Germany had recognised a similar right. THE EGYPTIAN FINANCIAL AGREEMENT. Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked the Government to postpone the consi- deration of the Egyptian financial agreement until after Easter.—Mr. GLADSTONE regretted not being able to do so, as the Government felt compelled to ask the definitive de- cision of the House on the subject before Easter. Discus- sion could be commenced either on Thursday or Monday week.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE considered the answer unsatifac- tory, and would repeat his question on Monday. ' THE Boaas.—Sir E. ASHLEY, replying to Mr. Redmond, I said the Government had every reason to believe that a Ipeaceful understanding would be arrived at with the Boers about disputed territory. I THE Rantsraustmow BILL—The House then went into committee on this bill. On farther consideration of the first schedule the Lord Advocate wished to explain the course Government proposed to take with regard to the amend- ments. It now appeared that it would not be in accordance with the agreement come to between the two great parties in the House. As they did not wish to do anything infring- ing that agreement, it was proposed to withdraw all Go- vernment amendments on the paper, and• not add any that would involve the merging of any Bcotch boroughs with counties, and on report it was proposed to withdraw the amendments of the character which had already been made in the schedule.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE thought the Lord Advocate had done right in putting the construction he had on what had transpired in committee on the bill last Wed- nesday.—Mr. A. ELLIOTT moved to report progress. He bad heard with greatest regret the announcement of the Lord Advocate.—Mr. Buchanan and Sir J. Hay also ex- pressed surprise.—After further discussion, the motion to report progress was rejected by 242 to 45.—Mr. DICK PEDDIE then moved an amendment to the schedule for re- arranging the Kilmarnock group of burghs by uniting it to Ayr, Lanark, Renfrew, and Dumbarton. The LORD- ADVOCATE opposed the amendment, which was negatived githout division.—Mr. A. GRANT urged the claims of Leith for separate representation, and moved an amendment to the schedule with that object.— Sir C. DUKE pointed out that the amendment could not be accepted without taking away a member from Perth. The second schedule, which gave list of boroughs that would lose one member, was next proposed. Mr. H. NORTH.. COTE moved to omit Exeter from the schedule. The amend- ment was negatived.--Mr. CALLAN moved the omission of Drogheda from the list of boroughs that were to cease to exist. MANTLES.—Some Mantle Shops have a disreputable system of ticketing Mantles in the window much tinder vs US, and this is often observed by Wires who purchase at the Mantle Co.'s Whol•eale Warehouse, which necessitates an ex- planation of this bad system. Ladies should know that Mantles prominently displayed, apparently under value, if secured might be bargains, but when marked under coat it is not intended they should be sold. These are made specially for the window sea draw, and probably so made as to fit no one, or are artfully changed for inferior copies hanging in readiness at the back of the window, of commoner materials and trimmings, in imitation of the one ticketed. This system is carried on with Black Costumes also. The Mantle Co. chal- lenge competition : but this false window display ne•ds ex- posure. Ladles who patronise the Mantle Co.'s Warehouse are guaranteed every satisfaction, and are certain of saving a large retail profit—The MANTLE CO.'s RETAIL STOCKROOM is 86, PICCADILLY, MANCHESTER ; no window (entrance next Cornish's.) IN PARLILDLENT.—Bassiox 1885. THE MANCHESTRE SHIP CANAL. WVHEREAS a MEETING of the OWNERS and RATEPAYERS of the Improvement Act District of Runcorn. in the County of Cheshire, we. held on Thursday, the sth day of February, 1885, in tha Bethesda School-room, Tioar-street. Runcorn, in pursuance of the Act of the 85th and 38th Tic., cap. 91, lotittned An Art to authorize the ap- plication of Funds of Municipal. Corporations and other govern- leg bodies in certain eases ;" And Whereas at the said Meeting, held at the time and place aforesaid, I. as Chairman of such meeting, and in stun- pliance with the statute, proposed the following resolution : " That the consent of the Owners and Ratepayers of the Im- provement Act Dlstr:ct of Runcorn be. and the same is hereby, give to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners to oppose In Parliament a Private Bill now before Parliament, Intituied, A Bill to authorize the construction of a Ship Canal to Man- chester, and for other purposes,' and this meeting hereby ap- proves and amnions the applying of the General District Rate, or other the Public Funds or Rates under the control of the said Improvement Commissioners, to the payment of the costs and expenses attending such opposition And Whereas the said resolution on being put to the meet- ing was not carried, whereupon demand was made that such question shottld be decided by a Poll of the Owners and Bate- payer.; And Whereas a Poll was accordingly taken in .rnahner pro- vided by the Public Health Act, 1875, and the Schedules thereto. I hereby declare that at such Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers, the above resolution was carried. Dated at Runcorn this 2nd day of March, 1885. ROBERT SHAW. Returning Officer.

PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED, HOLBORN BARS, LONDON.—THIRTY-81XTH AN- NUAL REPORT, for the year ending 31st DECEMBER, 1884. The Directors have much pleasure in presenting their report and a counts for the year 1884. The funds have been increased during the vet.r by the sum of 2862,606 • namely, In the Ordinary Branzli £158,840, and in the Industrial Branch £703,766, raising the total assets of the Company to £4,711,464. ORDINARY BRANCH. The new business of this branch for the year consists of 11,823 Policies, assm hag the sum of £1,359.361, and producing a New Annual Premium Income of £58,580. The Premiums of the year are £238,868, being an increase of £15,881 Over the year 1883. Ttie total increase for tb,e first three years of the Quinquennium is £97,611. The claims of the year amount to £112,474. The own- her of Deaths was 644, and 45 Endowment Assurances ma- tured. The rate of expenditure of the Branch slightly exceeds Ten per cent on the Premium Income. The number of Policies in force in this Branch is 51,835. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH. The Premiums received curing the year are £2,644,616, being an increase of £140,208. The Claims of the year amount to £l,O 3,273. The number of Deaths was 121,558. The number of Policies in force in this Branch is 6,302,89). The total expenses of the Branch show a reductioa in the rate of expenditure of fully Two per cent on the Premium In- come.
